Analysis of the results shows that, upon reaching quasi-static equilibrium, the merger remnant’s central region can be characterized as a differentially rotating CO star, comprising a slowly rotating cold core, a rapidly rotating hot envelope, and an outer centrifugally supported disc. To investigate its secular evolution, we construct a one-dimensional hydrodynamic stellar evolution model reproducing the SPH outcomes. Our calculations demonstrate that neutrino cooling at the core-envelope interface governs core growth, while carbon ignition in the envelope is avoided despite elevated effective accretion rates. This challenges the prevailing assumption of forced accretion of cold matter in earlier studies of double CO white dwarf merger remnants. Accordingly, our findings imply that certain merger products of double CO white dwarfs are viable progenitors of Type Ia supernovae, with a characteristic delay of approximately 10^5 years between the initial merger and subsequent explosion.

We analyze the weak-field, post-Newtonian expansion of solutions to the field equations in Chern-Simons gravity with a perfect fluid source, emphasizing their correspondence to the parameterized post-Newtonian (PPN) formalism up to first post-Newtonian (1 PN) order in the metric. Our results indicate that the PPN parameters in Chern-Simons gravity match those of general relativity, except for an additional term proportional to the Chern-Simons coupling parameter and involving the curl of the PPN vector potentials. This term is intrinsically enhanced by the nonlinear structure of spacetime, a phenomenon for which we provide a physical interpretation. By formulating this correction within the gravito-electro-magnetic framework, we examine its impact on the acceleration of point particles and the frame-dragging effect manifested in gyroscopic precession. These Chern-Simons-induced modifications to classical predictions thus present a viable avenue for current and future experimental efforts to constrain the fundamental parameters of Chern-Simons gravity and, by extension, related aspects of string theory.

Over the past two decades, the single-index model—a particular case of projection pursuit regression—has proven effective in addressing challenges inherent to high-dimensional nonparametric regression. This study examines the single-index prediction (SIP) model under weakly dependent samples, emphasizing its robustness to deviations from the classical single-index framework. The single-index is defined as the optimal approximation to the multivariate prediction function of the response variable, regardless of whether the true prediction function conforms to a genuine single-index form. We propose a polynomial spline estimator for the single-index prediction coefficients, establishing its root-n consistency and asymptotic normality. Estimation is achieved via an iterative optimization procedure that ensures computational efficiency sufficient to analyze large, high-dimensional datasets within seconds. Simulation studies provide strong empirical support consistent with the asymptotic theory. Application to Icelandic river flow data further demonstrates the method’s practical utility through superior out-of-sample rolling forecasts.

Air fluorescence detectors determine the energy of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays by capturing fluorescence light emitted from nitrogen molecules along the extensive air shower cascade. Accurate energy measurement necessitates correction of the detected light signal for atmospheric effects, which both attenuate the signal and introduce a significant background component from scattered Cherenkov light and multiple scattering. This correction requires regular evaluation of the aerosol attenuation length and the aerosol phase function, the latter defined as the angular probability distribution of scattered light. At the Pierre Auger Observatory in Malargue, Argentina, the aerosol phase function is measured hourly using two Aerosol Phase Function (APF) light sources. These sources project ultraviolet light beams across the fluorescence detectors’ field of view, enabling extraction of the phase function from images recorded by the fluorescence detector cameras. This paper provides a detailed account of the APF system’s design, current operational status, standard operating procedures, and performance evaluation at the Pierre Auger Observatory.

Close pre-main-sequence binary stars are predicted to carve central cavities within their protoplanetary disks; however, the extent to which material traverses the gap from the circumbinary disk to the individual circumstellar disks remains uncertain. In binaries with eccentric orbits, periodic perturbations of the outer disk are theorized to drive mass transfer across this gap, resulting in accretion modulated by the binary orbital period. This accretion may manifest as periodic luminosity fluctuations.

We investigate such periodic accretion in the pre-main-sequence spectroscopic binary UZ Tau E through BVRI photometry obtained over three years. The data reveal a distinct periodic brightness variation with a best-fit period of 19.16 ± 0.04 days, consistent with the refined spectroscopic binary period of 19.13 days derived from combined analysis of new and archival radial velocity measurements. Despite substantial stochastic variability, the dominant periodic signal presents as a broad luminosity enhancement spanning more than half the binary orbital cycle.

Variability in the H-alpha emission line is less definitively periodic; nevertheless, limited temporal sampling precludes exclusion of a periodic component. The observed photometric behavior aligns closely with predictions from numerical simulations of binaries possessing orbital parameters analogous to those of UZ Tau E. Collectively, these results provide compelling evidence for periodic accretion from circumbinary disks, which replenishes circumstellar disks and may extend the timescale available for planet formation.

Recent advances in characterizing real-world network structures have revealed that their evolution is governed by complex, multi-mechanism processes. A more detailed and realistic representation of these dynamics is thus essential for a comprehensive understanding of the structure and development of such complex systems. This study introduces a novel network growth rule integrating node addition and deletion and proposes an evolving network model to assess the impact of node deletion on network topology. Our findings demonstrate that node deletion substantially alters network structure: increasing its intensity induces a transition in the degree distribution from scale-free to exponential. Simultaneously, a nontrivial disassortative degree correlation arises spontaneously as an intrinsic consequence of network evolution within the model. Moreover, node deletion does not compromise network connectedness, provided the edge addition rate remains sufficiently high. Finally, node deletion attenuates—but does not abolish—the small-world effect typical of growing networks and generally reduces the clustering coefficient.

Objectives and Methodology: We report the results of 1.6 GHz Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations of nineteen GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources, fifteen selected from the Parkes Half Jansky (PHJ) sample (Snellen 2002) and four from a prior observational program. The study aimed to characterize the structural morphology of GPS sources, identify Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs), and examine the absorption mechanisms responsible for their characteristic convex radio spectra.

Findings: Total intensity 1.6 GHz VLBI images were obtained for seventeen sources for the first time. Approximately 80% exhibit a mini double-lobe morphology indicative of CSOs or CSO candidates, suggesting that their host active galactic nuclei (AGNs) are oriented edge-on relative to the observer. This indicates a high prevalence of mini double-lobe sources (or CSOs) within the PHJ sample. Specifically, six sources—J0323+0534, J1135-0021, J1352+0232, J2058+0540, J2123-0112, and J2325-0344—with measured redshifts and double-lobe structures under 1 kpc, are classified as CSOs. Conversely, three sources—J1057+0012, J1600-0037, and J1753+2750—are identified as core-jet sources based on their morphology and flux variability.

An advancement in magnetic force microscopy (MFM) spatial resolution employs sensor tips comprising carbon nanotubes grown at the apex of conventional silicon cantilever pyramids and coated with a thin ferromagnetic layer. Imaging high-density vertically recorded media with these tips reveals spatial frequency doubling under specific conditions. We demonstrate that this doubling results from switching of the magnetic moment direction within the nanotube tip, yielding a signal proportional to the absolute value of the conventional MFM signal. Computational modeling indicates that a substantial fraction of the tip volume undergoes this switching, suggesting the capability to image extremely high bit densities with nanotube-based magnetic force sensors.

We present a refined estimate of the local supermassive black hole (SMBH) mass function by integrating (i) the established empirical correlation between SMBH mass and the Sersic index of the host spheroidal stellar system, and (ii) the directly measured spheroid Sersic indices from 10,000 galaxies in the Millennium Galaxy Catalogue. This approach’s principal advantage lies in its observational simplicity and the direct use of the Sersic index as a reliable predictor of black hole mass, uniformly applicable to both elliptical galaxies and bulges of disc galaxies. This uniformity enables straightforward and precise SMBH mass estimations across early- and late-type galaxies. We characterize the SMBH mass function with a Schechter function, finding a logarithmic slope (1 + α) of approximately 0.7 for the full galaxy sample and about 1.0 for the early-type subset at the low-mass end. Restricting the analysis to spheroidal stellar systems brighter than M_B = –18 mag and integrating down to SMBH masses of 10^6 M_⊙, we derive local SMBH mass densities of ρ_bh,early-type = (3.5 ± 1.2) × 10^5 h_70^3 M_⊙ Mpc^–3 for early-type galaxies and ρ_bh,late-type = (1.0 ± 0.5) × 10^5 h_70^3 M_⊙ Mpc^–3 for late-type galaxies. These uncertainties are quantified via Monte Carlo simulations incorporating errors from the M_bh–n relation, the Sersic index catalogue, galaxy weighting schemes, and Malmquist bias. Combining these results yields a cosmological SMBH mass density of Ω_bh,total = (3.2 ± 1.2) × 10^–6 h_70. Accordingly, this novel and independent methodology indicates that (0.007 ± 0.003) h_70^3 percent of the universe’s baryonic matter is presently contained within supermassive black holes at galactic centers.

We investigate pion propagation in asymmetric nuclear matter (ANM), emphasizing the mode splitting among charged pion states. The analysis commences with a non-chiral framework describing pion-nucleon dynamics via pseudoscalar (PS) πN coupling, from which the pseudovector (PV) representation is obtained through nonlinear field transformations. Contributions from the Dirac sea are systematically evaluated in both formulations. Subsequently, results from a chiral effective Lagrangian approach are presented, incorporating short-distance Dirac vacuum effects through field parameter redefinition, consistent with the modern effective field theory framework. These findings are compared with prior calculations for symmetric nuclear matter (SNM). Finally, closed-form analytical expressions for effective pion masses and dispersion relations are derived employing the hard nucleon loop (HNL) approximation alongside an appropriate density expansion.

Employing the advanced full potential linearized augmented plane wave method, we investigate the emergence of a half-metallic phase in a ferromagnetic material. Ti substitution at the Ru sites in SrRuO3, a well-characterized ferromagnet, was performed to explore this phenomenon. Computational results confirm Ti4+ valence states, consistent with experimental data and analogous to those in SrTiO3. This substitution disrupts Ru–O–Ru connectivity, manifested as pronounced band narrowing and the formation of a finite energy gap between the t2g and eg bands. At 75% Ti substitution, a substantial gap exceeding 2 eV arises at the Fermi level (e_F) in the up-spin density of states, while down-spin states persist at e_F, characterizing the system as a half-metallic ferromagnet. Furthermore, tuning the Ti concentration allows precise modulation of the t2g–eg gap, effectively mitigating thermal effects that commonly limit high spin polarization at elevated temperatures in similar materials. This study thus presents a novel and straightforward strategy to induce half-metallicity in ferromagnetic materials, which are promising candidates for spintronic applications.

Medvinsky et al. [A. B. Medvinsky, I. A. Tikhonova, R. R. Aliev, B.-L. Li, Z.-S. Lin, and H. Malchow, Phys. Rev. E 64, 021915 (2001)] and Garvie et al. [M. R. Garvie and C. Trenchea, SIAM J. Control Optim. 46, 775–791 (2007)] demonstrated that a minimal spatially extended reaction-diffusion model of phytoplankton-zooplankton interactions can exhibit both regular and chaotic dynamics, as well as complex spatiotemporal patterns in patchy environments. Building on this foundation, the present study employs computational simulations and theoretical analysis to examine the model within parameter regimes corresponding to the mixed Turing-Hopf bifurcation. We identify spiral wave formation and show that spatiotemporal chaos arises from the far-field breakup of these spiral waves across extensive ranges of diffusion coefficients for both phytoplankton and zooplankton. Notably, this spatiotemporal chaos remains spatially localized and does not progressively invade the entire domain. These findings are corroborated by spectral computations and nonlinear bifurcation analyses of wave trains. Finally, we interpret the observed spatially structured patterns in terms of community-level ecological dynamics.

We analyze the pseudospectrum of a class of non-selfadjoint differential operators by examining the microlocal properties that govern spectral stability or instability under small perturbations of elliptic quadratic differential operators. These operators are defined via Weyl quantization of complex-valued elliptic quadratic symbols. Within this framework, we establish a concise necessary and sufficient condition on the Weyl symbol that ensures spectral stability. When this condition is not satisfied, we demonstrate the emergence of pronounced spectral instabilities at high energy levels, occurring in regions potentially far from the actual spectra. We furnish a detailed geometric characterization of these regions, thereby elucidating numerical observations of spurious eigenvalues detected by computational eigenvalue algorithms well beyond the true spectra.

We present detailed measurements of the transverse fluctuations of a string immersed in a turbulent air-jet flow, where these fluctuations arise from the fluctuating drag force that selectively excites harmonic modes over a range of wave-numbers. As a straightforward mechanical probe, the string facilitates scale-resolved, global characterization of the flow by capturing excitations at specific scales averaged over space and time. We further quantify the energy dissipation associated with the string’s motion and define the fluctuation-dissipation ratio (FDR) as the ratio of fluctuation amplitude to dissipative loss. Within this exploratory framework, the FDR is employed to define an effective temperature, which is critically compared with alternative turbulence-temperature constructs. Drawing on Kolmogorov’s 1941 phenomenology, we predict a –11/3 power-law exponent for the fluctuation spectrum. Our experimental results demonstrate close agreement with this theoretical prediction across the examined wave-number range and for Reynolds numbers from 7.4×10^4 to 1.7×10^5.

The product probability property, commonly termed statistical independence, is first examined to establish its foundational significance. Subsequently, generalized entropies are introduced as extensions of Shannon entropy. It is shown that the recursivity postulate fundamentally dictates the logarithmic functional form characteristic of Shannon entropy. This logarithmic structure inherently induces additivity in systems exhibiting the product probability property. Nevertheless, non-additivity is argued to be the more fundamental phenomenon, maintaining critical relevance—particularly in statistical mechanics—even under conditions of product probability property. Thus, additivity arises specifically from the incorporation of the recursivity postulate, which enforces a logarithmic form. The analysis then proceeds to consider entropy generalizations, including Mathai’s generalized entropy, with an examination of selected properties. Specific scenarios are explored wherein Mathai’s entropy yields pathway models, exponential and power-law behaviors, and associated differential equations. Moreover, the relationship between Mathai’s entropy and Kerridge’s measure of “inaccuracy” is investigated.

We examine the evolution of the electronic structure in SrRu_(1-x)Ti_xO_3 as a function of x via high-resolution photoemission spectroscopy. SrRuO_3 functions as a weakly correlated metal, while SrTiO_3 is a band insulator. Surface spectra reveal a metal-insulator transition at x = 0.5, marked by the formation of a soft gap, which progresses to a hard gap at higher x, consistent with transport data. In contrast, bulk spectra exhibit a pseudogap at the Fermi level and an atypical evolution characterized by an initial broadening of the coherent feature followed by a reduction in the lower Hubbard band intensity with increasing x. First-principles calculations accurately reproduce these anomalous high-energy-scale changes. Moreover, spectral lineshape analysis underscores a pronounced interplay between disorder and electron correlation that fundamentally governs the electronic properties of this system.

This paper addresses the solution of a unified fractional reaction-diffusion equation involving the Caputo derivative as the temporal operator and the Riesz-Feller fractional derivative as the spatial operator. Utilizing Laplace and Fourier transforms, the solution is obtained in closed form and expressed via the H-function. The results are comprehensive, encompassing prior work by Mainardi et al. (2001, 2005) on the fundamental solution of the space-time fractional diffusion equation, as well as by Saxena et al. (2006a, b) on fractional reaction-diffusion equations. The principal advantage of employing the Riesz-Feller derivative lies in its ability to unify the solution of the fractional reaction-diffusion equation with the fundamental solution of space-time fractional diffusion. This fundamental solution further generalizes neutral fractional diffusion, space-fractional diffusion, and time-fractional diffusion. These specialized diffusion processes can be interpreted as spatial probability density functions evolving temporally and are compactly represented in terms of H-functions.

In a previous study, the authors examined the implications of introducing a fifth large-scale space-time dimension into the orbital dynamics framework. This entailed reformulating, rather than modifying, Newtonian dynamics within a five-dimensional context, yielding predictions consistent with observed phenomena such as galactic flat rotation curves and the Pioneer Anomaly. An acceleration parameter, ar, was derived within this framework, playing a central role in the reformulated orbital dynamics equations, along with a proposed estimate of its magnitude.

Extending this work, the present companion paper reformulates the principle of conservation of energy within the same five-dimensional framework. This reformulation provides an alternative means to estimate ar, based exclusively on fundamental cosmological constants and parameters—most notably the gravitational constant, G—and independent of the orbital dynamics equations. Moreover, the analysis suggests that (i) the inverse square law of gravitation may fundamentally arise from energy conservation at the interface between the four-dimensional universe and the fifth large-scale space-time dimension, and (ii) a limiting case exists for the Tully-Fisher relation linking the speed of light to the Universe’s total mass.

Building upon the local philicity concept of Chattaraj et al. (Chattaraj, P. K.; Maiti, B.; Sarkar, U. J. Phys. Chem. A. 2003, 107, 4973) and the dual descriptor of Toro-Labbe and collaborators (Morell, C.; Grand, A.; Toro-Labbe, A. J. Phys. Chem. A. 2005, 109, 205), we propose a multiphilic descriptor that integrates these frameworks. Defined as the difference between the nucleophilic (Wk+) and electrophilic (Wk−) condensed philicity functions, this descriptor enables simultaneous evaluation of nucleophilicity and electrophilicity at distinct atomic sites within a molecule. We further examine the variation of these quantities along the reaction coordinate of a soft reaction, providing dynamic insight into reactivity changes. The descriptor’s predictive performance has been rigorously validated across selected molecular systems and reaction pathways. Additionally, corresponding force profiles have been analyzed in representative cases to elucidate underlying mechanistic features. To extend the analysis of intra- and intermolecular reactivities, we introduce and evaluate a related descriptor, nucleophilicity excess (ΔW−+), which quantifies the predominance of nucleophilicity over electrophilicity within a nucleophile; this descriptor has been applied specifically to all-metal aromatic compounds.

The layered structure and rheological properties of anti-wear films formed under rolling/sliding contact from lubricants containing zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDTP) and/or molybdenum dialkyldithiocarbamate (MoDTC) additives were examined via dynamic nanoindentation coupled with a simplified stiffness measurement model. Complementary local nano-friction experiments using the same apparatus assessed the evolution of the friction coefficient as a function of applied pressure across different lubricant formulations. For tribofilms composed solely of MoDTC, friction testing showed low applied pressures (<0.5 GPa) and correspondingly high apparent friction coefficients (μ > 0.4). In contrast, tribofilms containing both MoDTC and ZDTP exhibited an accommodation mechanism that increased applied pressure to several gigapascals, enabling the formation of a distinct low-friction domain (0.01 < μ < 0.05) located a few nanometers beneath the tribofilm surface. This marked friction reduction is attributed to the sliding of MoS2 planes in a favorable, well-aligned configuration, attainable only under sufficiently high pressure—a condition facilitated by the presence of ZDTP.

Despite extensive research on lattice Boltzmann (LB) methods, fundamental theoretical challenges persist. A principal issue is the formulation of a discrete kinetic theory that exactly recovers the fluid equations in a non-asymptotic manner, herein termed the LB inverse kinetic theory. This paper adopts a theoretical approach to develop such a framework. Although infinitely many solutions exist, this multiplicity can be exploited to satisfy critical criteria. Specifically, the discrete kinetic theory can be constructed to reproduce the fluid equations exactly for arbitrary non-equilibrium (yet suitably smooth) kinetic distribution functions, even arbitrarily close to the fluid domain boundaries. In contrast to prior entropic LB methods, the proposed theorem is established without imposing functional constraints on the initial distribution functions. Moreover, the paper presents explicit realizations of the theory alongside asymptotic approximations that enable determination of the fluid equations with prescribed accuracy. Consequently, asymptotic accuracy estimates for conventional LB approaches are derived, and a comparative analysis with the Chorin artificial compressibility method is provided.

This study investigates phonon-mediated transitions between translational energy levels of an atom subjected to a surface-induced potential. A general master equation is formulated to describe the evolution of the atom’s translational states. Within the Debye model framework, concise expressions for upward and downward transition rates are derived. Numerical calculations are performed for a deep silica-induced potential supporting numerous bound and free states of a cesium atom. The results demonstrate that, for deep bound levels, the total absorption rate is primarily governed by bound-to-bound transitions, whereas bound-to-free transitions predominate for shallow bound levels. Additionally, phonon emission and absorption rates are several orders of magnitude greater for deep bound levels than for shallow ones. Transitions originating from free states are also examined; for thermal cesium atoms at 100–400 μK near a silica surface maintained at 300 K, the adsorption rate (free-to-bound decay) is approximately twice the heating rate (free-to-free upward decay), while the cooling rate (free-to-free downward decay) is negligible.

Several giant HII regions exhibit soft diffuse X-ray emission, with the Carina nebula presenting the most intense such emission. The plasma temperature and thermal energy required to generate this emission can arise from collisions or termination shocks of fast stellar winds from main-sequence or embedded young O stars. Nevertheless, the extended X-ray emission frequently occurs in regions spatially detached from massive stellar clusters, rendering its origin uncertain.

The XIS CCD camera onboard Suzaku provides the highest spectral resolution currently available for extended soft X-ray sources, facilitating precise measurement of key emission lines within the soft X-ray band. Suzaku observed the Carina nebula’s core and its eastern sector (Car-D1) in August 2005 and June 2006, respectively. Spectra from the southern core and Car-D1 displayed prominent L-shell lines of iron ions and K-shell lines of silicon ions, whereas these features were markedly weaker in the northern core region.

Spectral fitting with an absorbed thin-thermal plasma model yielded plasma temperatures of approximately 0.2 and 0.6 keV and absorption column densities (NH) on the order of 1–2 × 10^21 cm^−2. Additionally, abundance variations by factors of roughly 2 to 3 were observed in oxygen, magnesium, silicon, and iron. Collectively, these findings indicate that the plasma may originate from either an ancient supernova or a supershell produced by multiple supernovae.

We report the results of a visible spectroscopic and photometric survey of Jupiter Trojans from multiple dynamical families, conducted with the ESO-NTT telescope. Our observations encompass 47 objects, comprising 23 from the L5 swarm and 24 from the L4 swarm. Combined with previously published data by Fornasier et al. (2004a) and Dotto et al. (2006), this dataset constitutes a comprehensive sample of visible spectra for 80 Trojans. This extensive collection facilitates detailed analysis of six families within the L5 cloud (Aneas, Anchises, Misenus, Phereclos, Sarpedon, Panthoos) and four within the L4 cloud (Eurybates, Menelaus, 1986 WD, and 1986 TS6).

The sample is predominantly composed of D-type asteroids, except for the Eurybates family in the L4 swarm, which is chiefly characterized by C- and P-type asteroids. All spectra are featureless, except for certain Eurybates members that exhibit a pronounced reflectance drop-off shortward of 5200 Å. This spectral characteristic closely parallels features observed in main belt C-type asteroids and is commonly attributed to intervalence charge transfer transitions involving oxidized iron.

Notably, our sample includes fainter and smaller Trojans than those typically reported, enabling the investigation of objects with estimated diameters below 40–50 km. Analysis of spectral slopes and colors as functions of diameter reveals indistinguishable size distributions between blue and red objects. Additionally, statistical analysis of spectral property distributions relative to orbital and physical parameters, compared with other minor body populations in the outer Solar System, indicates that Trojans with lower orbital inclinations exhibit significantly bluer spectra than those at higher inclinations; however, this inclination-dependent trend is primarily driven by the Eurybates family.

We present multifrequency VLBA observations of the final ten objects in a sample of FIRST-based compact steep spectrum (CSS) sources, selected to assess whether these represent relics of radio-loud AGNs that ceased activity at early evolutionary stages or exhibit intermittent activity. Initial 5 GHz observations were conducted with MERLIN, followed by VLBA observations at 1.7, 5, and 8.4 GHz in snapshot mode with phase-referencing. The resulting radio maps are presented alongside unpublished 8.4-GHz VLA images for five sources. Several objects exhibit complex radio morphologies, indicative of a convoluted evolutionary history that, in some cases, suggests intermittent activity. Notably, source 1045+352, a powerful radio- and infrared-luminous broad absorption line (BAL) quasar, displays an asymmetric two-sided morphology extending over several hundred parsecs in two distinct directions, further supporting intermittent activity. The compact structure and young age of 1045+352 are consistent with evolutionary models proposed for BAL quasars. Additionally, the submillimetre flux of 1045+352 is confirmed to be substantially contaminated by synchrotron emission.

The mechanical method of Abrikosov vortex-stimulated dynamics was employed to investigate relaxation phenomena in the vortex matter of high-temperature superconductors. This technique demonstrated that pulsed magnetic fields significantly influence relaxation processes within the vortex system. The study specifically assessed the effects of magnetic pulses with varying durations and amplitudes on the vortex system of the isotropic high-temperature superconductor HoBa2Cu3O7-δ, revealing threshold phenomena. Pulses below a critical duration did not affect relaxation behavior; however, exceeding this threshold induced a marked change in relaxation dynamics, evidenced by a stepwise variation in the relaxing mechanical moment. These results indicate that the formation time of the Abrikosov vortex lattice in HoBa2Cu3O7-δ is approximately 20 microseconds, roughly an order of magnitude longer than the formation time of a single vortex in type II superconductors.

We establish that the conditions underlying spin and pseudospin symmetries in the Dirac equation coincide with those yielding equivalent energy spectra for relativistic spin-1/2 and spin-0 particles in the presence of vector and scalar potentials. This equivalence is independent of the potentials' specific forms, indicating broad applicability across physics. Specifically, when both scalar and vector potentials are spherically symmetric, the isospectrality conditions eliminate the spin-orbit and Darwin terms in either the upper or lower component of the Dirac spinor. As a result, the spin-1/2 particle is energetically indistinguishable from a spin-0 particle. Moreover, under these conditions, the scalar particle shares not only the same energy but also the conserved orbital angular momentum corresponding to the relevant component of the spin-1/2 particle. Several potential applications of this correspondence are also discussed.

The classification of 38 halo white dwarf candidates identified by Oppenheimer et al. (2001) has been extensively debated. A key limitation of prior studies is the lack of trigonometric parallax measurements, which are essential for precise distance determinations. Accurate distances are critical for kinematically distinguishing halo white dwarfs from disk populations, thereby enabling more reliable estimates of the local density of halo dark matter within these stars.

Here, we present trigonometric parallax measurements for 15 candidate halo white dwarfs from the Oppenheimer et al. (2001) sample. Observations were performed with the ESO 1.56-m Danish Telescope and the ESO 2.2-m telescope between August 2001 and July 2004. Parallax accuracies of 1–2 milliarcseconds (mas) were achieved, corresponding to relative distance uncertainties of approximately 5% for six objects, 12% for three, and 20% for two. Four stars were likely beyond 100 parsecs, rendering their parallaxes unmeasurable within our observational sensitivity.

From these data, we derived distances, absolute magnitudes, and revised space velocities for the 15 candidates. Halo membership is conclusively confirmed for six objects, while five are more consistent with thick disk membership. For the remaining four, their large distances preclude definitive classification based solely on kinematics. Comparison with previously employed photometric parallaxes reveals a systematic overestimation of distances by photometric methods.

This dataset establishes a robust basis for revising the halo white dwarf space density, with a detailed analysis to be presented in a forthcoming publication.

Recent numerical studies have shown that rotating stars with pronounced differential rotation exhibit dynamical instability to bar-mode deformation at rotational kinetic to gravitational potential energy ratios as low as approximately 0.01. This instability is particularly pertinent to gravitational wave astronomy, notably regarding high-frequency sources such as core-collapse supernovae. Here, we present high-resolution simulations employing an adaptive mesh refinement hydrodynamics code to investigate the low T/|W| bar-mode instability. Our results elucidate the complex morphological features driving the instability’s nonlinear dynamics, demonstrating that the excitation of Kelvin-Helmholtz-like fluid modes beyond the star’s corotation radius induces saturation of the bar-mode deformation. While corroborating general trends from prior studies, we further establish that numerical resolution critically influences the long-term nonlinear evolution of the instability. These findings bear significant implications for the accurate modeling of rotating star dynamics and the determination of maximal gravitational wave amplitudes.

Population structure, shaped by spatial embedding and broader interaction networks such as model social networks, fundamentally affects the dynamics and outcomes of evolutionary games. These effects, however, often depend sensitively on specific features of the underlying topology and dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce a minimal population structure defined by two hierarchical levels of interaction, which effectively isolates the influence of spatial structure from detailed topological configurations. Starting from individual-level stochastic processes, we derive the system’s governing dynamics through two successive mean-field approximations. Within this framework, interaction topology is characterized by two parameters: the effective local population size and the relative strength of local dynamics versus global mixing. We demonstrate, for example, a continuous transition to cooperation dominance in populations with hierarchical unstructured mixing when the benefit-to-cost ratio falls below the local population size. Applying this spatial structure model to the repeated prisoner's dilemma reveals a novel, counterintuitive mechanism whereby a continuous influx of defectors sustains cooperation. Further exploration of the phase space for both the repeated prisoner's dilemma and the rock-paper-scissors game uncovers complex structural dynamics and reproduces phenomena observed in other spatially explicit models, including biodiversity maintenance and the emergence of global oscillations.

This study examines the impact of inhomogeneous mass density on the frequencies and wave profiles of torsional Alfvén oscillations in solar coronal loops. Dispersion relations are analytically derived for the asymptotic limits of weak and strong inhomogeneity and validated by numerical solutions spanning a broad range of inhomogeneity strengths. The analysis reveals that inhomogeneous mass density reduces torsional oscillation frequencies relative to estimates based on apex density, a consequence of decreased average Alfvén speed due to enhanced density at the loop footpoints. These dispersion relations and wave profiles are essential for interpreting prospective observations of torsional oscillations, which appear as periodic spectral linewidth modulations. Accordingly, torsional oscillations provide a robust diagnostic tool for advancing coronal seismology.

Certain rate-1/2 partially systematic parallel concatenated convolutional codes (PCCCs) exhibit lower error floors than their rate-1/3 parent codes. Nonetheless, identifying optimal puncturing patterns necessitates exhaustive search, and convergence to low bit error rates is impeded when the systematic output of a rate-1/2 partially systematic PCCC undergoes heavy puncturing. This study introduces and rigorously analyzes a class of rate-1/2 partially systematic PCCCs, designated pseudo-randomly punctured codes. Their bit error rate performance is evaluated, demonstrating consistently lower error floors relative to their rate-1/3 parent codes. Furthermore, comparison of analytical predictions with simulation results confirms reliable convergence to the error floor region, attributable to moderate puncturing of the systematic output. These findings support pseudo-random puncturing as an effective approach to enhance bandwidth efficiency while reducing the error floor of PCCCs.

This study addresses the problem of limit shapes in the six-vertex model with domain wall boundary conditions by analyzing the emptiness formation probability, a specifically constructed bulk correlation function. We present a closed-form expression for this function, formulated both as a determinant and as a multiple integral, facilitating a comprehensive investigation of the model’s limit shapes across the full range of vertex weights. Notably, for vertex weights along the free-fermion line of the phase diagram, we establish the equivalence of the emptiness formation probability to a one-matrix model with a triple logarithmic singularity, known as the Triple Penner model. Saddle-point analysis of this matrix model yields the Arctic Circle Theorem and its extension to Arctic Ellipses, results previously recognized in the context of domino tilings.

This paper presents a thorough analysis of the geometries induced by a gravitating generalized Yang monopole in even-dimensional spacetimes, with emphasis on configurations exhibiting both black hole and cosmological horizons. These two-horizon systems are thermally unstable, causing thermalization to drive the horizons toward coalescence. The study focuses on this limiting case, demonstrating that although the coordinate separation between the horizons approaches zero, the physical distance remains finite. Consequently, a residual spacetime region persists, whose geometry is explicitly derived and identified as a generalized Nariai solution. The thermal properties of this emergent spacetime are subsequently examined. Furthermore, the paper investigates the elliptical relationship between the radii of spheres within the geometry and critically discusses the inclusion or exclusion of a mass-type term in the line element.

We report temperature-dependent infrared response measurements of the quasi-one-dimensional organic conductor (TMTSF)₂SO₃, conducted both parallel (E||a) and perpendicular (E||b') to the stacking axis. Above the metal-insulator transition, attributed to anion ordering, the optical conductivity spectra exhibit Drude-like behavior. Upon cooling below this transition, an energy gap of approximately 1500 cm⁻¹ (185 meV) opens, manifesting as a charge transfer band in the optical conductivity. Analysis of infrared-active vibrational modes reveals long-range crystal structure modulation below the transition temperature, alongside short-range lattice modulation fluctuations above it. Furthermore, we identify a novel infrared mode near 710 cm⁻¹, characterized by an atypical temperature dependence not previously observed in other (TMTSF)₂X salts undergoing metal-insulator transitions. To account for this anomalous behavior, we propose a qualitative model invoking coupling between TMTSF molecular vibrations and reorientation of the electric dipole moment of the FSO₃ anion.

The generation of microwave-frequency oscillations constitutes a principal anticipated application of spintronic devices exploiting spin transfer. We report transport and microwave power measurements on purpose-designed nanopillars exhibiting a theoretically predicted, non-standard “wavy” angular dependence of the spin transfer torque. Consistent with these models, our experiments reveal a novel current-induced dynamic regime characterized by large-angle magnetization precessions in the absence of any applied magnetic field. By obviating the need for an external field, such non-standard nanopillars offer a promising avenue for the realization of spin transfer oscillators driven solely by intrinsic torque effects. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for refining theoretical descriptions of the torque’s angular dependence.

Mn3V2O8 is a magnetic system comprising S = 5/2 Mn2+ ions arranged in a kagome-staircase lattice. We constructed its magnetic phase diagram for temperatures above 2 K and magnetic fields up to 9 T through systematic magnetization and specific heat measurements with the field oriented along the three crystallographically distinct lattice directions. At low fields, the system undergoes magnetic ordering below Tm1 ≈ 21 K, followed by a second phase transition at Tm2 ≈ 15 K. Additionally, a phase transition detected exclusively by specific heat measurements—but absent in magnetization—is observed for all field orientations, converging toward Tm2 as the field approaches zero. The magnetic response exhibits pronounced anisotropy, with critical fields defining phase boundaries markedly higher when the field is applied perpendicular rather than parallel to the kagome-staircase plane. Consequently, the field-temperature (H–T) phase diagrams are intricate, revealing seven distinct magnetic phases.

This paper addresses the challenge of estimating the unconditional distribution of a post-model-selection estimator, a sequential two-step process involving model selection—via methods such as a model selection criterion (e.g., AIC) or hypothesis testing—followed by parameter estimation of the selected model, typically through least squares or maximum likelihood, using the same dataset. We establish that accurate estimation of this unconditional distribution is fundamentally infeasible, even asymptotically. Specifically, we prove that no estimator attains uniform consistency for this distribution, including local uniform consistency. This result follows from local minimax lower bounds on estimator performance, measured by the probability that the estimation error exceeds a predetermined threshold. These bounds converge to values of 1/2 or even 1 as sample size increases, contingent on the context. Furthermore, analogous impossibility results apply to the distribution of linear functions of the post-model-selection estimator, such as predictors.

We analyze nine years of Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer observations of Seyfert 1 and 1.2 galaxies to investigate correlations among their X-ray spectral features. The dataset comprises 350 time-resolved spectra from 12 galaxies of these types. Each spectrum is modeled as an intrinsic power-law X-ray continuum originating near the central black hole, subsequently reprocessed and absorbed by circumnuclear material. To evaluate result robustness, Monte Carlo simulations were performed on the spectral sample. We identify a nuanced relationship between the iron line equivalent width (EW) and the power-law photon index (Γ), exhibiting a positive correlation up to approximately Γ ≲ 2, beyond which it reverses to a weak anti-correlation at steeper photon indices. This pattern is interpreted as dilution of the disk spectrum—including the narrow iron line—by a beamed jet component, highlighting its potential as a diagnostic of jet dominance. Additionally, the sample shows a pronounced correlation between the reflection fraction (R) and Γ; however, this is attributed primarily to modeling degeneracies rather than an intrinsic physical association. Finally, the canonical X-ray Baldwin effect—an anti-correlation between the 2–10 keV X-ray luminosity and EW—is observed across the entire sample but is absent within individual galaxies or subtypes.

We analyze the relic density \( n_\chi \) of non-relativistic, long-lived, or stable particles \(\chi\) within non-standard cosmological frameworks. Assuming that thermally produced \(\chi\) particles constitute the dark matter energy density, we compute the relic abundance from arbitrary initial temperatures during the radiation-dominated epoch and establish a universal lower bound on the initial temperature, \( T_0 \geq m_\chi/23 \), independent of the \(\chi\) annihilation cross section. Furthermore, we examine cosmological scenarios with modified expansion rates, demonstrating that an approximate formula structurally analogous to the standard expression accurately predicts the final relic abundance in these contexts. By fixing the \(\chi\) annihilation cross section to reproduce the observed cold dark matter abundance within the standard cosmological model, we constrain potential deviations in the expansion rate at temperatures near \( T \sim m_\chi/20 \), well before the onset of Big Bang nucleosynthesis.

We present a thorough reanalysis of leptogenesis via the out-of-equilibrium decay of the lightest right-handed neutrino within type II seesaw frameworks, explicitly incorporating flavour-dependent effects. In these frameworks, the light neutrino mass matrix receives contributions from both the conventional type I seesaw term and an additional direct mass term induced by the vacuum expectation value of a Higgs triplet. This supplementary contribution is examined using both a specific Higgs triplet model and a model-independent effective approach. By systematically deriving bounds on flavour-specific decay asymmetries, the mass of the lightest right-handed neutrino, and the early universe’s reheat temperature, we compare these constraints with those obtained in the type I seesaw scenario. Our findings demonstrate that flavour-dependent thermal leptogenesis in type II seesaw models becomes increasingly efficient with rising light neutrino mass scale, thereby relaxing the associated bounds, whereas the type I seesaw framework is subject to more stringent constraints. We further emphasize that flavour-dependent effects are essential and must be incorporated in leptogenesis analyses within type II seesaw contexts.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the Galaxy Stellar Mass Function (GSMF) up to redshift z = 2.5, based on data from the VVDS survey. Stellar masses are estimated from broad-band photometry employing two distinct assumptions regarding star formation histories; notably, incorporating secondary bursts into a continuous star formation history systematically increases stellar mass estimates by up to 40%. At low redshift (z = 0.2), we identify a significant population of low-mass galaxies (<10^9 M_⊙), predominantly faint blue galaxies characterized by M_I − M_K ≈ 0.3.

The GSMF evolves gradually up to z ≈ 0.9, beyond which more pronounced changes occur. Despite this evolution, a massive tail of galaxies exhibiting extremely red colors (M_I − M_K = 0.7–0.8) persists up to z = 2.5. Across all mass ranges, the overall galaxy number density declines with increasing redshift; for instance, galaxies with M > 10^8 M_⊙ show a 59 ± 5% reduction at z = 1. Concurrently, a mild mass-dependent evolutionary trend consistent with "mass-downsizing" emerges: massive galaxies (M > 6 × 10^10 M_⊙) exhibit mild or negligible (<30%) evolution up to z = 0.7, whereas less massive systems are incompatible with a no-evolution scenario.

By z = 1, a substantial fraction (≥50%) of massive galaxies have assembled the majority of their stellar mass, having converted most of their gas into stars, thereby excluding "dry mergers" as the dominant assembly mechanism below this redshift. This fraction declines to approximately 33% at z = 2. In contrast, low-mass systems undergo a continuous decline in both number density and stellar mass density—by up to a factor of four—from the present epoch to z = 2, consistent with ongoing mass assembly processes extending to z < 1.

Linear polarization in X- and gamma-rays constitutes a critical diagnostic for various astrophysical sources by elucidating their geometry, magnetic field configurations, and radiation mechanisms. Despite theoretical predictions of energy-dependent polarization signatures, empirical X-ray polarization measurements remain limited and predominantly confined to mono-energetic detections. This study evaluates the feasibility of detecting energy-dependent polarization via the Compton scattering technique, focusing on the proposed PoGOLite balloon experiment operating within the 25–100 keV energy range. We conduct Geant4 simulations of a PoGOLite instrument model incorporating photon spectra from Cygnus X-1 and accreting magnetic pulsars, each at an intensity of 100 mCrab. These simulations correspond to effective exposure times of 6 and 35 hours, representing standard and extended-duration flights, respectively. Both gradual and abrupt variations in polarization as functions of energy are systematically analyzed and rigorously compared to constant polarization scenarios using chi-square statistical tests. Results demonstrate that, for the Cygnus X-1 spectrum in its hard state, the null hypothesis of constant polarization across energy can be statistically rejected assuming a fully polarized reflected component; however, this discrimination is not achievable at lower polarization fractions. In the case of the accreting pulsar, constant polarization can be excluded when polarization is confined to a narrow energy band with a polarization degree of at least 50%, or when exhibiting a negative step change from 30% to 0%.

Observations of stellar activity cycles offer a distinctive opportunity to investigate magnetic dynamos across a wide range of physical conditions. Forthcoming space-based asteroseismology missions, equipped with sufficient sensitivity to detect oscillation frequency shifts induced by magnetic variations, are anticipated to deliver critical constraints on the internal environments sustaining these cycles. To predict such frequency shifts, we have developed a method that scales variations in the Mg II activity index relative to solar data. Applying this method to the solar-type subgiant beta Hyi, we analyze archival spectra from the International Ultraviolet Explorer in conjunction with two epochs of ground-based asteroseismic observations. The results provide qualitative evidence supporting the predicted frequency shifts and enable the determination of optimal timing for future asteroseismic measurements of this star.

Swift detected a precursor to the main burst of GRB 061121 (z = 1.314), enabling comprehensive multiwavelength observations from optical to gamma-ray bands. Additional data were obtained from Konus-Wind, XMM-Newton, ROTSE, and the Faulkes Telescope North. The gamma-ray, X-ray, and UV/optical emissions peaked approximately 75 seconds post-trigger; however, the optical and X-ray afterglow components appeared earlier, either preceding or coinciding with this peak. Spectral evolution was evident throughout the burst, with the prompt emission exhibiting a pronounced positive correlation between brightness and spectral hardness. The Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) of the prompt emission, spanning 1 eV to 1 MeV, displayed a flat profile with a flux density maximum near 1 keV. At this stage, the optical-to-X-ray spectra were better modeled by a broken power-law than by a single power-law, consistent with prior observations of X-ray flares. As the afterglow progressed, the SED exhibited spectral hardening, potentially indicative of self-Comptonisation; however, this interpretation requires circumstellar densities comparable to those in molecular cloud cores. The afterglow decay proceeded more slowly than predicted by standard theoretical models. Despite differing spectral lags between precursor and main emission phases, both conformed to the lag-luminosity correlation characteristic of long-duration bursts. GRB 061121 is the instantaneously brightest long burst detected by Swift to date. Combining Swift and Konus-Wind data, we estimate an isotropic energy release of 2.8 × 10^53 erg over the 1 keV to 10 MeV range in the GRB rest frame. A probable jet break at approximately 2 × 10^5 seconds implies a beaming-corrected gamma-ray energy of approximately 10^51 erg.

In recent decades, scholarly interest in the Burgers equation has intensified, particularly concerning extensions of the original one-dimensional pressureless model introduced in the 1930s by J.M. Burgers. A significant portion of this research has focused on Burgers turbulence, involving the analysis of solutions to the one- or multi-dimensional Burgers equation under random initial conditions or stochastic forcing. This focus has been driven by the expanding applications of the Burgers model in statistical physics, cosmology, and fluid dynamics. Recognized as a fundamental paradigm of nonlinear systems operating far from equilibrium, Burgers turbulence has catalyzed substantial advances in several areas, including the study of random Lagrangian systems, the theory of stochastic partial differential equations and their invariant measures, dynamical systems theory, and the application of field-theoretic methods to elucidate dissipative anomalies and multiscaling phenomena in hydrodynamic turbulence. This review provides a cohesive synthesis of selected contributions from these interdisciplinary fields.

The focusing performance of X-ray optics, typically quantified by the Half Energy Width (HEW), is principally determined by mirror deformations and photon scattering arising from the microroughness of reflecting surfaces. The contribution of X-ray Scattering (XRS) to the HEW, denoted as H(E), generally increases with photon energy E. Consequently, XRS is anticipated to be the principal limiting factor in forthcoming hard X-ray imaging telescopes—such as SIMBOL-X, NeXT, Constellation-X, and XEUS—that operate above 10 keV.

Previous investigations have evaluated the scattering contribution to the HEW by characterizing surface microroughness via its Power Spectral Density (PSD), grounded in the established theory of X-ray scattering from rough surfaces. Building upon this framework, we propose an analytical approach that directly converts a given surface roughness PSD into an H(E) profile and, conversely, translates an H(E) performance requirement into the corresponding PSD. This PSD thus defines the maximum permissible microroughness necessary to satisfy the H(E) criterion throughout the telescope’s operational energy band.

Employing this methodology, we have developed an analytical and broadly applicable formalism that computes the XRS contribution to the HEW directly from the surface PSD, contingent on PSD measurements spanning a wide range of spatial frequencies. Moreover, we have addressed the inverse problem, enabling immediate derivation of the mirror surface PSD from an empirically obtained H(E) function. This formalism further facilitates determination of the maximum allowable PSD levels required to fulfill a specified H(E) performance target.

To initiate the analysis of electromagnetic meson production reactions within the nucleon resonance region, we determine the hadronic interaction parameters of a dynamical coupled-channel model developed in *Physics Reports* 439, 193 (2007) by fitting πN scattering data. The model explicitly incorporates the πN, ηN, and ππN channels, with the ππN channel further resolved into the resonant components πΔ, ρN, and σN. Non-resonant meson-baryon interactions are derived from Lagrangians via a unitary transformation method, ensuring theoretical consistency. One or two bare excited nucleon states are included in each of the S, P, D, and F partial waves to generate resonant amplitudes during fitting. Model parameters are initially constrained by fitting empirical πN elastic scattering amplitudes from SAID up to 2 GeV and subsequently refined and validated through direct comparison of predicted differential cross sections and target polarization asymmetries with original data from the elastic π^± p → π^± p and charge-exchange π^- p → π^0 n processes. Furthermore, the model’s predicted total cross sections for πN reactions and the πN → ηN reaction demonstrate good agreement with experimental measurements. Finally, applications of the constructed model to the analysis of electromagnetic meson production data and its prospects for future development are discussed.

At a distance of 725 pc, the Cepheus A East star-forming region provides an optimal environment for the study of massive star formation. Previous morphological analyses have suggested that the flattened molecular gas distribution surrounding the young stellar object (YSO) HW2 corresponds to a massive protostellar disk with an approximate radius of 350 AU. To elucidate the nature of this structure, we employed the Plateau de Bure Interferometer to acquire (sub-)arcsecond-resolution images of high-density and shock tracers—specifically methyl cyanide (CH3CN) and silicon monoxide (SiO)—centered on HW2. At a spatial scale of 1 arcsecond (~725 AU), the observed flattened molecular gas distribution is best explained as the projected superposition of at least three protostellar objects within the plane of the sky, one of which drives a molecular outflow oriented at a small angle relative to the line of sight. Although the presence of a protostellar disk around HW2 cannot be conclusively excluded, its detection is likely confined to smaller spatial scales or reliant upon observations employing alternative molecular tracers.

A two-step density-matrix renormalization group method is employed to investigate the anisotropic two-dimensional Hubbard model. The numerical approach is first validated by benchmarking against exact solutions of the tight-binding model, achieving agreement in ground-state energy to four decimal places for system sizes up to \(24 \times 25\). The method is then extended to the interacting regime. Under strong Hubbard interactions, the ground state is predominantly characterized by magnetic correlations that remain robust despite significant frustration. In this regime, interchain pair tunneling in both singlet and triplet channels is negligible and unaffected by frustration. Conversely, at weak Hubbard couplings, interchain non-local singlet pair tunneling is enhanced, coinciding with a pronounced suppression of magnetic correlations. Collectively, these findings indicate the potential emergence of a superconducting ground state in the weak-coupling limit.

Red clump giants (RCGs) in the Galactic bulge serve as approximate standard candles and thus provide reliable distance indicators. Utilizing the proper motion catalogue from the second phase of the Optical Gravitational Microlensing Experiment (OGLE-II; Sumi et al. 2004), we calculate proper motion dispersions of RCGs across 45 distinct fields. The substantial sample size of 577,736 stars enables determination of proper motion dispersions with precision on the order of a few percent. These empirical measurements are subsequently compared to predictions from a state-of-the-art particle simulation of the Galactic bulge. Although the simulation generally aligns with the observational data, it consistently overestimates the anisotropy of the velocity ellipsoid. Moreover, significant field-to-field variations in proper motion dispersions are observed, which may reflect intrinsic astrophysical heterogeneity or result from unidentified systematic errors.

We present theoretical arguments, corroborated by numerical evidence, confirming the existence of long-range intrachain correlations in concentrated solutions and melts of long, flexible polymers. These correlations induce a systematic swelling of short chain segments, arising from the melt’s incompressibility. This incompressibility generates an effective repulsion between connected segments, quantitatively expressed as \( u(s) \approx \frac{s}{\rho R^3(s)} \approx \frac{c_e}{\sqrt{s}} \), where \( s \) denotes the curvilinear segment length, \( R(s) \) its characteristic spatial size, \( c_e \approx \frac{1}{\rho b_e^3} \) the swelling coefficient, \( b_e \) the effective bond length, and \( \rho \) the monomer density. The relative deviation of the segmental size distribution from ideal Gaussian behavior scales proportionally with \( u(s) \). Analysis of multiple moments of this distribution yields precise estimates of \( b_e \) and \( c_e \) for asymptotically long chains. Contrary to the short-range decay predicted by Flory’s ideality hypothesis, the bond-bond correlation function between two bonds separated by \( s \) monomers exhibits an algebraic decay proportional to \( 1/s^{3/2} \). Lastly, the influence of finite chain length on these correlations is briefly addressed.

The linearized relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (RMHD) equations are derived for a uniform, axially magnetized cylindrical relativistic jet spine embedded within a uniform, axially magnetized sheath moving at relativistic velocity. To accurately represent phenomena associated with Alfvén wave propagation approaching the speed of light, these equations explicitly incorporate the displacement current. This formulation yields a dispersion relation governing the normal modes. Analytical solutions in the low- and high-frequency limits facilitate the derivation of a comprehensive stability criterion, demonstrating that the relativistic jet spine can remain stable against velocity shear-driven Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities in both trans-Alfvénic and super-Alfvénic regimes. Furthermore, the resonance condition corresponding to the maximal growth rate of the normal modes is determined for kinetically and magnetically dominated regimes. Numerical solutions of the dispersion relation validate the analytical results and are employed to explore parameter spaces characterized by elevated sound and Alfvén speeds.

Over the past two decades, significant advances in understanding quantum transport far from equilibrium have yielded a conceptual framework synthesizing the Landauer approach with the non-equilibrium Green function (NEGF) method. This integrated framework is now widely applied in the analysis and design of nanoscale devices, providing a unified theoretical description that encompasses a broad range of device types—including molecular conductors, carbon nanotubes, and silicon transistors—and spans transport regimes from ballistic to diffusive. In this presentation, a simplified variant of this model is employed to investigate a specifically engineered device functioning as an electronic Maxwell’s demon, which selectively facilitates electron flow in a preferred direction. The primary objective is to elucidate the fundamental roles of contacts and demons in quantum transport and energy conversion. Although the discussion remains theoretical and abstracts from practical complexities, the illustrative devices considered fall within current technological capabilities. For example, recent experimental studies of thermoelectric phenomena in molecular conductors align closely with predictions derived from the model. The Maxwell’s demon device examined closely resembles the pentalayer spin-torque device extensively studied by multiple research groups; however, to our knowledge, its potential application as a nanoscale heat engine or refrigerator, as proposed herein, has not been previously addressed. It is essential to emphasize that the aim is not to assess practical implementations but to present a clear, tractable model demonstrating how out-of-equilibrium demons, when suitably integrated into nano-devices, can facilitate energy conversion.

We investigate the mixing time of a systematic scan Markov chain devised to sample uniformly from the set of proper 7-colourings of a finite rectangular sub-grid of the infinite square lattice, hereafter termed the grid. The chain operates by sequentially cycling through finite vertex subsets arranged in a predetermined order, applying a heat-bath procedure to update the colours within each subset. These subsets specifically consist of 2×2 sub-grids. Employing a computer-assisted proof, we establish that the chain achieves mixing within O(log n) scans, where n denotes the sub-grid size. Our methodology incorporates a heuristic to compute the requisite couplings between colourings on these 2×2 sub-grids. Crucially, this study provides the first rigorous proof of rapid mixing for a systematic scan Markov chain on the grid with fewer than eight colours. Furthermore, we present partial results that highlight the considerable challenges inherent in proving rapid mixing for systematic scan chains sampling 6-colourings of the grid, based on analyses of 2×3 and 3×3 sub-grids.

Planetary topography may be conceptualized either as a load borne by the lithosphere or as a dynamic response arising from lithospheric flexure driven by mantle convection. In both frameworks, the lithosphere’s mechanical behavior under external forces is rigorously described by the theory of thin elastic plates or shells. For one-plate planets, the spherical geometry of the lithospheric shell critically governs the flexural response. Existing formulations of the governing equations for deformations and stresses in spherical shells, however, have been confined to the assumption of uniform shell thickness. In contrast, localized analyses of gravity and topography data reveal pronounced lateral heterogeneities in lithospheric thickness.

This study derives scalar flexure equations governing the deformation of a thin spherical shell exhibiting spatial variability in thickness or Young’s modulus. These equations are generally amenable to sequential solution, except for a coupled system of two simultaneous equations whose solutions correspond to transverse deflection and an associated stress function. To incorporate basal loading induced by mantle convection, the classical stress function framework is extended to accommodate loads with a toroidal tangential component. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that toroidal tangential displacement necessarily arises in the presence of shell thickness variations, even in the absence of explicit toroidal loading. Finally, the degree-one harmonic components of both transverse deflection and toroidal tangential displacement are shown to be invariant with respect to the shell’s elastic properties and correspond to rigid-body translational and rotational modes.

The flexure equations developed herein for shells with variable thickness are indispensable for predicting gravity anomalies in local admittance analyses and for constructing stress maps relevant to tectonic investigations.

We present XMM-Newton observations of the candidate magnetar CXOU J164710.2-455216, obtained 4.3 days prior to and 1.5 days following two notable events detected by Swift on 21 September 2006: (1) a 20 ms burst releasing 10^37 erg within the 15–150 keV range, and (2) a rapid spin-down glitch marked by a fractional period change of 10^−4. During this interval, the pulsar’s luminosity increased by a factor of 100, from 10^33 to 10^35 erg s^−1 in the 0.5–8.0 keV band, accompanied by spectral hardening. Concurrently, the pulsed count rate in this energy range rose tenfold, while the fractional root-mean-square amplitude of the pulses declined from 65% to 11%. Additionally, the pulse profile evolved from a single peak to a complex three-peaked morphology. Comparable phenomena have been documented in other magnetars following outbursts, notably 1E 2259+586 in June 2002. We interpret these findings as evidence that plastic deformation of the neutron star’s crust induced a subtle twist in the external magnetic field, which generated magnetospheric currents responsible for the observed X-ray outburst.

The decreasing intrinsic redshift (DIR) model asserts that galaxies originate as compact objects ejected from the nuclei of mature active galactic nuclei (AGN), characterized by substantial intrinsic redshift components, \( z_i \). These nascent AGN, identified as quasars, initially exhibit luminosities several magnitudes lower than those of mature galaxies. Over approximately \(10^8\) years, the decline in \( z_i \) coincides with a commensurate increase in luminosity, culminating in their evolution into mature AGN classes such as Seyfert and radio galaxies. The evidence presented herein demonstrates that low- and intermediate-redshift AGN are sub-luminous relative to radio galaxies, thereby providing robust empirical support for the DIR model. This finding further implies that high-redshift AGN (quasars) are similarly sub-luminous, with their apparent luminosities elevated above those of radio galaxies on a \(\log z\)–\(m_v\) diagram due to the presence of a significant intrinsic redshift component. Moreover, an increase in luminosity is observed below \( z = 0.06 \), which the DIR framework attributes to source maturation and associated luminosity enhancement. Conversely, if this luminosity increase is genuine, it poses interpretative challenges for the cosmological redshift (CR) model, as such low redshifts are unlikely to correspond to elevated star formation rates or increased material availability for galaxy formation. The potential for selection effects within the CR model to account for these observations is also examined.

This study presents new light curves and derives the rotational periods and phase functions of several large Kuiper Belt objects, including the dwarf planet Eris (2003 UB313). The object (120348) 2004 TY364 exhibits a double-peaked light curve with a period of 11.70 ± 0.01 hours and a peak-to-peak amplitude of 0.22 ± 0.02 magnitudes. Similarly, (84922) 2003 VS2 displays a well-defined double-peaked light curve characterized by a period of 7.41 ± 0.02 hours and a magnitude variation of 0.21 ± 0.02. In contrast, (126154) 2001 YH140 shows variability of 0.21 ± 0.04 magnitudes, potentially corresponding to a single-peaked period of 13.25 ± 0.2 hours.

Among the sample, seven additional Kuiper Belt objects—2001 UQ18, (55565) 2002 AW197, (119979) 2002 WC19, (120132) 2003 FY128, (136108) Eris, (90482) Orcus (2004 DW), and (90568) 2004 GV9—exhibit no statistically significant brightness variations on short rotational timescales within measurement uncertainties. Notably, three medium to large-sized objects—2004 TY364, Orcus, and 2004 GV9—demonstrate relatively steep linear phase curves, with slopes ranging from approximately 0.18 to 0.26 magnitudes per degree over phase angles between 0.1 and 1.5 degrees. By contrast, the exceptionally large dwarf planet Eris exhibits a markedly shallower phase curve slope of 0.09 ± 0.03 magnitudes per degree, closely resembling that of Pluto.

These observations suggest that the surface properties of the largest dwarf planets in the Kuiper Belt systematically differ from those of smaller objects, likely reflecting their enhanced capacity to retain volatile ices and sustain tenuous atmospheres. Moreover, absolute magnitudes derived from the measured phase slopes differ by several tenths of a magnitude from those reported by the Minor Planet Center, highlighting the critical importance of precise phase function characterization for accurate determination of intrinsic brightness.

This review addresses the phenomenon of parity doubling in excited hadrons, characterized by parity degeneracy first experimentally identified nearly four decades ago. Recent experimental findings on light mesons have stimulated renewed interest and intensified investigation into this unresolved phenomenon. To provide a comprehensive introduction, the analysis traces the historical development of parity doubling, commencing with foundational theoretical frameworks from the 1960s—such as Regge theory and dynamical symmetries—and advancing to contemporary developments, including broader degeneracy patterns and the AdS/QCD framework. The review systematically traces the evolution of theoretical interpretations and critically evaluates experimental evidence within the non-strange hadron sector. Furthermore, several 1960s experiments targeting missing non-strange bosons are revisited, with their results argued to be promising when reassessed in light of current understanding.

Let \( L \) be an ample holomorphic line bundle over a compact complex Hermitian manifold \( X \). A fixed smooth Hermitian metric on \( L \) induces a Hilbert space structure on the space of global holomorphic sections valued in the \( k \)-th tensor power of \( L \). This paper establishes convergence results for the associated Bergman kernels as \( k \to \infty \), with convergence precisely characterized by the equilibrium metric linked to the fixed metric and the Monge–Ampère measure of the fixed metric restricted to a designated support set. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the equilibrium metric has Lipschitz continuous first derivatives. These results extend classical theorems pertaining to the case of positive curvature of the fixed metric, wherein the equilibrium metric coincides with the fixed metric itself.

High-resolution spectroscopy of U Gem during quiescence revealed the absence of a hot spot or gas stream at the accretion disk’s outer edge, contrary to prior expectations. Instead, a prominent narrow emission feature was detected near the secondary star. The radial velocity curve, derived from the wings of the double-peaked H\(\alpha\) emission line, exhibited a semi-amplitude consistent with ultraviolet measurements reported by Sion et al. (1998).

To enhance the detection of absorption or emission features from the late-type companion, we introduce a novel method for determining \(K_2\). Our results closely correspond with previously published values obtained from the near-infrared Na I doublet. Additionally, comparative analysis of the TiO band with those of late-type M stars identifies an M6V spectral type as the optimal fit, contributing approximately 5% of the total flux in this spectral region.

Assuming the measured radial velocity semi-amplitudes accurately trace the orbital motions of the binary components, we combine our values—\(K_{\mathrm{em}} = 107 \pm 2\) km s\(^{-1}\) and \(K_{\mathrm{abs}} = 310 \pm 5\) km s\(^{-1}\)—with the inclination angle \(i = 69.7 \pm 0.7^\circ\) from Zhang and Robinson (1987) to derive system parameters: a white dwarf mass \(M_{\mathrm{WD}} = 1.20 \pm 0.05\, M_\odot\), a red dwarf mass \(M_{\mathrm{RD}} = 0.42 \pm 0.04\, M_\odot\), and an orbital separation \(a = 1.55 \pm 0.02\, R_\odot\).

Analysis of the double emission peak separation yields an outer disk radius \(R_{\mathrm{out}}/a \approx 0.61\), closely approaching the inner Lagrangian point at \(L_1/a \approx 0.63\). This proximity implies that, at the time of observation, the accretion disk filled the primary’s Roche lobe, and material escaping through \(L_1\) collided directly with the disk, thereby generating the observed hot spot.

Employing series expansion techniques, we examine the ground state properties and excitation spectra of hard-core bosons at half filling on square and triangular lattices. Nearest-neighbor repulsive interactions induce short-range density order at the antiferromagnetic wavevector, coinciding with the emergence of a roton minimum in the density excitation spectrum. On the square lattice, the model corresponds to the extensively studied XXZ model, wherein the roton gap closes precisely at the Heisenberg symmetry point, yielding the characteristic excitation spectrum of the Heisenberg antiferromagnet. Conversely, on the triangular lattice, the closure of the roton gap signals the onset of the supersolid phase. Our results further indicate that the transition from the superfluid to the supersolid phase is likely weakly first order. Additionally, we identify distinct features in the density of states—namely, two pronounced peaks and a sharp discontinuity—that may be experimentally accessible.

We present an analysis of cometary X-ray spectra employing an extended version of our charge exchange emission model (Bodewits et al. 2006). This model was applied to eight comets observed with the Chandra X-ray Observatory and ACIS spectrometer across the 300–1000 eV energy range. The sample—comprising C/1999 S4 (LINEAR), C/1999 T1 (McNaught-Hartley), C/2000 WM1 (LINEAR), 153P/2002 (Ikeya-Zhang), 2P/2003 (Encke), C/2001 Q4 (NEAT), 9P/2005 (Tempel 1), and 73P/2006-B (Schwassmann-Wachmann 3)—represents a diverse array of cometary types, solar wind conditions, and observational contexts.

Our interaction model integrates state-selective and velocity-dependent charge exchange cross sections, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of the dependence of cometary X-ray emission on intrinsic cometary properties, observational parameters, and solar wind characteristics. We demonstrate that cometary X-ray spectra predominantly reflect the local solar wind environment. By fitting the Chandra observations within the constraints of the charge exchange model, we directly derived relative solar wind ion abundances from the spectra. This analysis reveals that spectral variations correspond to distinct solar wind regimes, facilitating classification of comet interactions into three categories: (I) fast, cold wind; (II) slow, warm wind; and (III) disturbed, fast, hot winds associated with interplanetary coronal mass ejections. Furthermore, we predict a fourth spectral class associated with the cool, fast solar wind characteristic of high-latitude regions.

This letter examines acceleration in a flat cosmological model incorporating a conformally coupled phantom field, identifying acceleration as an inherent characteristic of the model. The dynamics are reformulated as a three-dimensional dynamical system, with analysis concentrated on an invariant two-dimensional submanifold. Within this framework, the concordance Friedmann–Robertson–Walker (FRW) model with cosmological constant \(\Lambda\) emerges as a global attractor on the invariant manifold. The system’s behavior near this attractor is then analyzed and shown to be accurately approximated by the linearized dynamics. Our results demonstrate that trajectories of the conformally coupled phantom scalar field with a simple quadratic potential cross the cosmological constant barrier infinitely many times in phase space. Moreover, the universal behavior of both the scalar field and its potential is derived.
