Collectively, these findings indicate that the phantom scalar field conformally coupled to gravity naturally induces a dynamical mechanism concentrating the equation of state parameter near the critical value \(w_{\text{eff}} = -1\). Finally, we characterize a pathway to the cosmological constant \(\Lambda\) marked by infinitely repeated crossings of the phantom divide \(w_{\text{eff}} = -1\).

Short-lived radionuclides, notably ^60Fe (half-life = 1.5 Myr), present in the early Solar System most plausibly originated from a nearby supernova. Conventional models attribute the initiation of the Sun’s primordial molecular cloud collapse to a supernova shock. Alternatively, we propose that the protoplanetary disk was already established when a proximate (<1 pc) supernova directly injected radioactive material into it. To evaluate this hypothesis, we conducted the first numerical simulations addressing two critical questions: whether such a close supernova would destroy the disk and whether any ejecta would be assimilated. Our results demonstrate that the disk does not acquire sufficient momentum from the shock to overcome the protostar’s gravitational binding. Resultant mass loss is minimal (<1%), primarily due to stripping induced by Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities at the disk surface, which concurrently facilitate incorporation of approximately 1% of the intercepted ejecta. These low efficiencies of disk disruption and material injection arise from the disk’s elevated internal pressure, which impedes deep penetration of the ejecta before stalling. Accordingly, injection of gas-phase ejecta alone is insufficient to explain the radionuclide abundances observed in meteorites. We contend that radionuclides condensed into dust grains within the supernova ejecta, and that such grains would be incorporated into the disk with near-complete efficiency. Thus, the meteoritic abundances of short-lived radionuclides such as ^60Fe are consistent with the injection of dust grains condensed from the ejecta of a nearby (<1 pc) supernova into an already-formed protoplanetary disk.

In supergravity, one-parameter solutions characterized by scalars and a metric define curves on the scalar manifold that correspond to geodesic trajectories in ungauged supergravity. Although geodesic motion is typically associated with the absence of a scalar potential, it is well established that such trajectories may also occur in the presence of a scalar potential for time-dependent solutions, particularly within scaling cosmologies. This study extends the analysis of these solutions by examining them within the framework of pseudo-supersymmetry in multi-field systems, deriving the relevant first-order equations via a Bogomol'nyi-like method. We demonstrate that scaling solutions exhibiting pseudo-BPS properties necessarily correspond to geodesic curves. Moreover, we clarify the method for solving the geodesic equations of motion when the scalar manifold constitutes a maximally non-compact coset, as encountered in maximal supergravity, by employing a parametrization of the coset in the Borel gauge. To illustrate the practical application of these results, we analyze cosmological solutions derived from higher-dimensional gravity compactified on an \( n \)-torus.

We investigate the impact of Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) peculiar velocities on cosmological parameter estimation by analyzing published distant and local SN Ia samples from the Supernova Legacy Survey first-year cosmology report. While prior studies commonly assume the No Flow model—where local SNe are stationary relative to the cosmic microwave background (CMB) frame—we critically assess this assumption by applying peculiar velocity corrections to local SNe using three distinct flow models derived from the IRAS PSCz galaxy redshift survey. These models, characterized by varying β values (β = Ω_m^0.6 / b), accurately reproduce the Local Group’s motion relative to the CMB frame. Utilizing these velocity-corrected datasets, we fit for the dark energy equation of state parameter w, the matter density parameter Ω_m, and the cosmological constant density parameter Ω_Λ under flatness or ΛCDM cosmological assumptions, incorporating a baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) prior. The χ² statistic quantifies the influence of velocity corrections on fit quality. Among the models considered, the β = 0.5 flow model is most strongly favored, yielding a significantly improved fit relative to the No Flow assumption, consistent with previous peculiar velocity analyses. Comparing the No Flow assumption with the preferred flow models, we identify the largest potential systematic error in w due to neglecting peculiar velocities as Δw = +0.04, with corresponding uncertainties ΔΩ_Λ = -0.04 and ΔΩ_m < +0.01. The favored β = 0.5 model produces parameter estimates of w = -1.08 (+0.09, -0.08) and Ω_m = 0.27 (+0.02, -0.02) assuming a flat cosmology, and Ω_Λ = 0.80 (+0.08, -0.07) with Ω_m = 0.27 (+0.02, -0.02) assuming a ΛCDM cosmology with w fixed at -1.

Within the interacting electron model Hamiltonian for the one-dimensional 1/4-filled band, the singlet ground state adopts a Wigner crystal configuration solely when the nearest-neighbor electron-electron repulsion exceeds a critical threshold. We demonstrate that this critical Coulomb interaction varies with the spin subspace, decreasing as the spin quantum number increases. Consequently, upon cooling, the system may transition from the Wigner crystal charge-ordered phase to a spin-Peierls state, characterized as a Bond-Charge-Density Wave with charge occupancies distinct from those of the Wigner crystal. This transition is facilitated by the intrinsic coupling between spin excitations and modulations in site charge density within the spin-Peierls state of the 1/4-filled band. We apply this theoretical framework to quasi-one-dimensional organic charge-transfer solids exhibiting a 1/4-filled band, with particular focus on 2:1 tetramethyltetrathiafulvalene (TMTTF) and tetramethyltetraselenafulvalene (TMTSF) cationic salts. We contend that recent experimental findings provide compelling evidence for the Wigner crystal to Bond-Charge-Density Wave transition in multiple members of the TMTTF family. Furthermore, our theory elucidates the coexistence of two distinct antiferromagnetic phases alongside a single spin-Peierls state within the generic phase diagram of 2:1 cationic solids. Specifically, the antiferromagnetic phases exhibit charge occupancies characteristic of either the Wigner crystal or the Bond-Charge-Spin-Density Wave, whereas the spin-Peierls state consistently corresponds to the Bond-Charge-Density Wave.

In a previous study (Gavignaud et al. 2006), we introduced a sample of type-1 Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) derived from the first epoch of the VIMOS-VLT Deep Survey (VVDS). This sample comprises 130 faint, broad-line AGN with redshifts up to z = 5 and apparent magnitudes between 17.5 and 24.0, selected based on their spectral characteristics. In the present work, we measure the Optical Luminosity Function (OLF) up to z = 3.6 from this sample and systematically compare these results with those obtained from brighter AGN samples at both low and high redshifts. Owing to its extension more than one magnitude fainter than previous optical surveys, our data provide robust constraints on the faint end of the luminosity function at high redshift.

To extend coverage in luminosity and redshift, we combine the faint VVDS sample with a substantial bright AGN sample from SDSS DR3 (Richards et al., 2006b) and evaluate multiple evolutionary models. Our analysis identifies a luminosity-dependent density evolution (LDDE) model as the optimal representation of the combined luminosity functions across a broad range of redshifts and luminosities. This model, consistent with those derived from major X-ray surveys, permits the redshift of the AGN space density peak to vary as a function of luminosity, thereby accounting for the observed excess of faint AGN within the redshift interval 1.0 < z < 1.5.

Applying this LDDE framework, we demonstrate for the first time using optically selected samples that the peak of AGN space density shifts significantly toward lower redshifts with decreasing luminosity. This finding, previously reported in multiple X-ray selected samples, substantiates the "AGN cosmic downsizing" paradigm, wherein the space density of more luminous AGN—presumably associated with more massive black holes—reaches its maximum earlier in cosmic history than that of lower luminosity AGN.

This paper critically evaluates the singularity theorems of Penrose, Hawking, and Geroch by demonstrating that, during gravitational collapse, a black hole acts as an ultrahigh-energy particle accelerator, elevating particle energies well beyond those attainable in terrestrial facilities. When particle energies \( E \) reach approximately \( 10^{2} \) GeV or higher—corresponding to temperatures \( T \) near \( 10^{15} \) K—the matter undergoes a complete phase transition into a quark-gluon plasma permeated by leptons. Given that quarks and leptons are fermions, Pauli’s exclusion principle prevents further collapse into a space-time singularity. Consequently, it is proposed that the ultimate fate of a black hole may involve stabilization as a quark star, oscillation as a pulsating quark star potentially emitting gravitational radiation, or an explosive event analogous to a mini bang.

We present a kinetically constrained lattice gas model that rigorously enforces chain connectivity to investigate the dynamics of a single polymer chain confined within a two-dimensional cell. Employing this model, we conduct Monte Carlo simulations to systematically characterize polymer dynamics across a broad density range. Notably, even near the fully packed configuration, monomers continue to diffuse throughout the cell, achieving root mean square displacements comparable to the cell dimensions. This diffusion transpires over timescales during which the polymer’s global conformation remains predominantly preserved. To quantitatively evaluate this shape persistence, we define a local tangent field and analyze the two-time tangent-tangent correlation function, which exhibits glass-like dynamics indicative of slow structural relaxation. Furthermore, in both closed and open chain topologies, we observe reptational motion and morphological reshaping driven by localized fingering events that facilitate global monomer displacement while maintaining chain connectivity.

We quantified the flux, spatial distribution, color, and substructure of diffuse intracluster light (ICL) in a sample of ten galaxy clusters spanning a broad range of mass, morphology, redshift, and density. Deep, wide-field imaging was acquired in two photometric bands using the one-meter Swope and 2.5-meter du Pont telescopes at Las Campanas Observatory. To ensure measurement accuracy, data reduction and analysis rigorously addressed illumination correction, background subtraction, point spread function characterization, and galaxy subtraction. ICL flux was detected in both bands across all clusters, ranging from 7.6 × 10^{10} to 7.0 × 10^{11} h^{-1} solar luminosities in the r-band and from 1.4 × 10^{10} to 1.2 × 10^{11} h^{-1} solar luminosities in the B-band. These fluxes constitute 6–22% of the total cluster light within one quarter of the virial radius in the r-band and 4–21% in the B-band. The mean ICL B–r colors, corrected for k-correction and evolutionary effects to the present epoch, range from 1.5 to 2.8 magnitudes. Furthermore, in several clusters, ICL is detected both near the cluster center and within group environments extending up to approximately 1 h^{-1} Mpc from the center. The sample, drawn from the Abell catalog, is incomplete, excluding high-redshift clusters characterized by low density, flux, or mass, as well as low-redshift clusters exhibiting high flux, mass, or density. This selection bias complicates the interpretation of correlations between ICL flux and cluster properties. Nonetheless, the presence of a cD galaxy correlates with centrally concentrated galaxy distributions and ICL profiles, supporting formation scenarios in which the ICL originates either from galaxy interactions at the cluster center or from earlier processes within groups that subsequently merge there.

Fluctuations in molecular abundances within living cells markedly affect cellular growth and homeostasis. Specifically, variations in the expression levels of regulatory molecules—such as signaling proteins and transcription factors—propagate through downstream targets within molecular networks, thereby modulating their dynamics. To elucidate the mechanisms underlying the emergence of noise correlations in these systems, we develop an analytical framework centered on metabolic pathways, which are densely interconnected and whose structural and functional organization may be constrained by noise characteristics.

Exploiting the formal analogy between the dynamics of a linear metabolic pathway and those of an exactly solvable linear queueing network or mass-transfer system, we derive explicit expressions characterizing fluctuations in intermediate metabolite concentrations across several prototypical metabolic motifs. Our analysis demonstrates that, with the exception of one motif, steady-state fluctuations at distinct nodes remain effectively uncorrelated. This finding indicates that variations in enzyme levels influence only the local segment of the pathway where the enzyme acts, without propagating noise to other network regions. Consequently, intermediate metabolites can be shared among multiple reactions without facilitating widespread noise transmission.

The analytical framework presented is extendable to metabolic networks with more complex topologies, as well as to protein-signaling networks governed by analogous biochemical kinetics. Furthermore, we discuss potential implications of these results for the bioinformatic analysis of metabolomic datasets.

Context: Investigating planets within open clusters is essential for elucidating the influence of dynamical environments on planetary formation and evolution. Aims: Motivated by the established correlation between stellar metallicity and planet occurrence rates, this study targeted the metal-rich, old open cluster NGC 6791 to detect close-in planets via the transit method. Methods: A ten-night observational campaign was conducted using the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope (3.6 m), the San Pedro Mártir telescope (2.1 m), and the Loiano telescope (1.5 m). To enhance transit detection likelihood, these data were combined with observations from the eight-night campaign by Bruntt et al. (2003). The photometric precision attained was sufficient for identifying planetary transits. Results: Assuming that the frequency and characteristics of close-in planets in NGC 6791 are comparable to those of field stars with similar metallicity, simulations predicted the detection of 2–3 transiting planets. However, the transit candidates previously reported by Bruntt et al. (2003) were not confirmed. The probability that this null detection resulted from chance is estimated between 3% and 10%, depending on the cluster’s assumed metallicity. Conclusions: The absence of detected transits may reflect (i) a reduced occurrence rate of close-in planets in star clusters, (ii) smaller planetary radii associated with planets orbiting super metal-rich stars, or (iii) limitations inherent in the underlying assumptions. Definitive constraints on planet frequency in NGC 6791 require more extensive photometric monitoring with 3–4 m class telescopes.

At redshifts z > 5.7, a substantial fraction of Lyman Alpha (Lyα) emitting galaxies (LAEs) exhibit rest-frame equivalent widths (EW) exceeding approximately 100 Å. Given that only a minor fraction of the Lyα flux produced by these galaxies is transmitted through the intergalactic medium (IGM), their intrinsic Lyα EWs must exceed the theoretical maximum predicted for a population-II stellar population with a Salpeter initial mass function. To elucidate the mechanisms driving Lyα emission in these high-redshift galaxies, we propose a simplified model wherein galaxies first undergo a burst of very massive star formation, producing a large intrinsic EW, followed by a subsequent phase dominated by population-II star formation with a lower EW.

We evaluate this model against an extensive set of high-redshift observations and demonstrate its ability to reproduce eight key properties of the galaxy population using plausible parameters for star formation efficiency and duration. These properties include: (i–iv) the ultraviolet (UV) and Lyα luminosity functions of LAEs at z = 5.7 and 6.5; (v–vi) the mean and variance of the EW distribution among Lyα-selected galaxies at z = 5.7; (vii) the EW distribution of i-dropout galaxies at approximately z ~ 6; and (viii) the empirically observed correlation between stellar age and EW.

Our results indicate that accounting for the anomalously large intrinsic equivalent widths necessitates a burst of very massive star formation lasting no more than a few to ten percent of the galaxy’s star-forming lifetime. This intense star formation episode may signify the presence of population-III stars in a small fraction of i-drop galaxies and in roughly half of the Lyα-selected galaxy population.

This study rigorously investigates azimuthal structures commonly associated with elliptic and directed flow by employing two-dimensional (2D) angular autocorrelations to precisely separate nonflow contributions—predominantly minijets—from authentic flow phenomena. To this end, the Fourier-transform framework of azimuthal structure is extended to incorporate power spectra and autocorrelations, which are mathematically linked via the Wiener-Khintchine theorem. Within this expanded framework, conventional flow analysis methodologies are critically evaluated, and the influence of reaction plane estimation on flow characterization is examined. The 2D angular autocorrelation technique is then introduced, with its application demonstrated using empirical data and its efficacy validated through a simulation study that distinctly isolates flow and nonflow components. Furthermore, it is shown that an alternative correlation metric based on Pearson’s normalized covariance provides a more intuitive and robust quantification of azimuthal structure.

Information integration applications, including mediators and mashups, rely on users to manually discover and integrate information resources—a labor-intensive task necessitated by the need to navigate results generated through keyword-based searches. Although current search methodologies exploit evidence from document contents, metadata, and the content and link structures of referring pages, they remain insufficient for effectively indexing information sources commonly termed the "hidden Web," which dynamically generate documents in response to queries. Conversely, social bookmarking platforms have recently gained prominence by enabling users to annotate and share metadata across diverse information sources, thereby providing rich evidence that facilitates resource discovery. This paper introduces a probabilistic model of the user annotation process within the social bookmarking system del.icio.us and applies this model to automatically identify resources pertinent to a specific information domain. Experimental results derived from del.icio.us data demonstrate that this approach constitutes a promising method for automating resource discovery.

Flickr, a social media platform, facilitates photo uploading, tag-based annotation, group submissions, and the formation of social networks through user contacts. Among its browsing and search features, tag-based search retrieves all images associated with a given keyword. However, when the keyword is ambiguous—for example, "beetle," which may denote either an insect or a car—tag search frequently returns numerous images irrelevant to the user’s intended meaning. We hypothesize that users convey their photographic interests through the metadata they provide, including contacts and image annotations. By leveraging this metadata, we demonstrate methods to personalize search results, thereby enhancing retrieval effectiveness. First, we show that filtering tag search results by a user’s contacts or an expanded social network comprising contacts of contacts significantly improves search precision. Subsequently, we introduce a probabilistic model that exploits tag information to uncover latent topics within the search results. Because users’ interests are also reflected in the tags they assign to their own images, the latent topics identified by the model enable personalized search by prioritizing images aligned with the user’s topical preferences.

This study addresses the resummation of substantial logarithmic perturbative corrections to the single-inclusive jet cross section at hadron colliders, emphasizing the region near the partonic threshold where incoming partons have marginally sufficient energy to produce a high-transverse-momentum final state. The structure of these logarithmic corrections is critically influenced by the treatment of the jet’s invariant mass at threshold. We incorporate a non-zero jet mass at threshold, thereby enhancing the fidelity of the representation of experimental conditions. By matching our results to existing semi-analytical next-to-leading-order calculations, we derive resummed expressions accurate to next-to-leading logarithmic order. Additionally, numerical results are presented to quantify the impact of resummation effects at Tevatron and RHIC energies.

We resolve a longstanding open problem in algorithmic game theory by proving that Bimatrix—the problem of computing a Nash equilibrium in a two-player game—is complete for the complexity class PPAD (Polynomial Parity Argument, Directed version), as introduced by Papadimitriou (1991). This foundational result initiates a systematic investigation into the computational complexity of Nash equilibria. Specifically, we prove that Bimatrix does not admit a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme unless all problems in PPAD are solvable in polynomial time. Furthermore, we establish that the smoothed complexity of the classical Lemke-Howson algorithm—and, more generally, of any algorithm solving Bimatrix—is super-polynomial unless every problem in PPAD is solvable in randomized polynomial time. Collectively, these results demonstrate that, even within the simplest class of non-cooperative games, the computational tasks of finding and approximating equilibria are polynomial-time equivalent to fixed point computation. Moreover, our findings yield two significant complexity-theoretic implications in mathematical economics and operations research: computing Arrow-Debreu market equilibria is PPAD-hard, and the P-Matrix Linear Complementarity Problem is computationally more demanding than convex programming unless all PPAD problems admit polynomial-time algorithms.

This study rigorously examines the equation of state (EOS) for a perfectly conducting, relativistic magnetized fluid by systematically contrasting the widely employed ideal constant-\(\Gamma\) law EOS—commonly used in astrophysical applications—with a more physically accurate EOS that better characterizes a single-species relativistic gas. The analysis focuses on three principal aspects that clarify the conceptual underpinnings of EOS selection. First, it assesses the impact of adopting a realistic EOS on the propagation of fast magneto-sonic shocks, thereby challenging the applicability of the constant-\(\Gamma\) law EOS in scenarios exhibiting pronounced temperature gradients across hydromagnetic waves. Second, it introduces an innovative inversion technique for recovering primitive variables, such as rest-mass density and pressure, from conservative variables. This technique is compatible with a general EOS and effectively mitigates catastrophic numerical cancellations in both non-relativistic and ultrarelativistic regimes, ensuring numerical stability. Finally, the study presents selected astrophysically relevant numerical simulations—including magnetized accretion flows around Kerr black holes—to evaluate the influence of various EOS formulations on the resulting solutions. The principal finding demonstrates that employing a realistic EOS substantially enhances solution accuracy during transitions between cold and hot gas phases, whereas reliance on a polytropic EOS under such conditions may significantly compromise solution fidelity.

This study presents a comprehensive model elucidating the evolution and self-assembly of randomly oriented carbon nanotubes (CNTs) grown as a thin film on a metallic substrate for field emission within a diode configuration. Although these thin film devices initially demonstrate high output, they typically exhibit significant current decay over time. To clarify this behavior, the model first establishes a nucleation-coupled degradation mechanism describing CNT deterioration via fragmentation and cluster formation. Subsequently, it integrates the random orientation of CNTs with their electromechanical interactions to accurately capture the self-assembly dynamics. CNT orientation is then updated by accounting for both their degraded state and the electromechanical forces acting upon them. At the device scale, field emission current is computed using the Fowler-Nordheim equation, with integration performed over the computational cell surfaces on the anode side. The simulation results show strong concordance with experimental data. Employing this framework, numerical simulations systematically examine the influence of various geometric parameters and their statistical characteristics on the temporal evolution of device current.

Transition objects—young stars distinguished by an optically thin inner disc and an optically thick outer disc—exhibit properties indicative of substantial disc evolution. To elucidate their nature, we compare their stellar accretion rates (Ṁ) and disc masses (M_disc) with those of accreting T Tauri stars of similar age. Our analysis demonstrates that transition objects in Taurus occupy a distinct locus within the Ṁ versus M_disc parameter space. Specifically, compared to non-transition single stars in Taurus, transition objects exhibit stellar accretion rates approximately an order of magnitude lower at comparable disc masses, while their median disc masses are roughly four times greater. These characteristics are consistent with predictions from multiple planet formation theories, suggesting that the formation of Jovian-mass planets plays a significant role in the origin of some transition objects. Furthermore, by designating transition objects as a distinct demographic group among accreting T Tauri stars, we identify a stronger correlation between disc mass and stellar accretion rate, with a slope approaching unity, in agreement with simplified disc accretion models.

Carbon nanotubes (CNTs), owing to their distinctive properties, have emerged as promising candidates for field emission devices. Experimental investigations, however, reveal significant variability in their field emission performance, underscoring the necessity for rigorous analysis of these discrepancies. Addressing this challenge requires designing efficient field-emitting devices via a systematic multiphysics modeling framework that integrates the relevant governing mechanisms. In this study, we develop such a model for randomly oriented CNTs within a thin film by coupling the field emission process, electron-phonon transport, and the mechanical behavior of individual isolated CNTs. To capture dynamic behavior, we implement a computational scheme that incrementally updates the CNT states over time. Finally, the device current is computed using the Fowler-Nordheim equation to evaluate performance at the device scale.

Let \( z = (z_1, \ldots, z_n) \) and denote by \( \Delta = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial^2}{\partial z_i^2} \) the Laplace operator. A formal power series \( P(z) \) is termed Hessian Nilpotent (HN) if its Hessian matrix \( \mathrm{Hes}\,P(z) = \left( \frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial z_i \partial z_j} \right) \) is nilpotent. Recent studies [BE1], [M], and [Z] have established that the Jacobian conjecture is equivalent to the vanishing conjecture (VC) for HN polynomials. Specifically, for any homogeneous HN polynomial \( P(z) \) of degree \( d=4 \), the identity \( \Delta^m P^{m+1}(z) = 0 \) holds for all sufficiently large integers \( m \).

In the first part of this paper, we prove that the VC holds for every homogeneous HN polynomial \( P(z) \) under the geometric assumption that the projective subvarieties \( \mathcal{Z}_P \) and \( \mathcal{Z}_{\sigma_2} \) in \( \mathbb{CP}^{n-1} \)—defined respectively by the principal ideals generated by \( P(z) \) and by \( \sigma_2(z) := \sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2 \)—intersect exclusively at regular points of \( \mathcal{Z}_P \). This intersection condition provides a geometric framework guaranteeing the vanishing property. Consequently, the Jacobian conjecture holds for symmetric polynomial maps of the form \( F(z) = z - \nabla P(z) \) with \( P(z) \) HN, provided \( F \) admits no nonzero fixed point \( w \in \mathbb{C}^n \) satisfying \( \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2 = 0 \).

In the second part, we establish an equivalent characterization of the VC for arbitrary HN formal power series \( P(z) \). We demonstrate that the vanishing condition \( \Delta^m P^{m+1}(z) = 0 \) for all sufficiently large \( m \) is equivalent to the stronger statement that, for every polynomial \( f(z) \), the expression \( \Delta^m \big( f(z) P(z)^m \big) \) also vanishes for all sufficiently large \( m \). This equivalence broadens the functional context in which the vanishing phenomenon associated with Hessian nilpotency may be analyzed.

Recent advances [BE1], [Me], and [Z2] have reduced the Jacobian Conjecture (JC) ([BCW], [E]) to a vanishing conjecture (VC) involving Laplace operators and Hessian nilpotent (HN) polynomials, characterized by nilpotent Hessian matrices. This paper first establishes that this VC, and consequently the JC, is equivalent to a more general VC formulated for all second-order homogeneous differential operators \(\Lambda\) and \(\Lambda\)-nilpotent polynomials \(P\), where \(\Lambda\)-nilpotency is defined by the condition \(\Lambda^{m} P^{m} = 0\) for every \(m \geq 1\). Building on this equivalence, we reinterpret several well-established results concerning the JC, HN polynomials, and the VC for Laplace operators as analogous statements pertaining to \(\Lambda\)-nilpotent polynomials and the associated VC for arbitrary second-order homogeneous differential operators \(\Lambda\). This analysis also functions as a concise survey of HN polynomials and the related VC within this unified framework. Finally, we investigate a still partially unresolved connection between general \(\Lambda\)-nilpotent polynomials and classical orthogonal polynomials in one or multiple variables, thereby providing a conceptual foundation for understanding the isotropic properties exhibited by homogeneous \(\Lambda\)-nilpotent polynomials associated with second-order homogeneous full-rank differential operators \(\Lambda\) possessing constant coefficients.

A k-query Locally Decodable Code (LDC) encodes an n-bit message \( x \) into an N-bit codeword \( C(x) \) such that any specific bit \( x_i \) of \( x \) can be probabilistically recovered by querying only k bits of \( C(x) \), even when a constant fraction of the codeword bits is corrupted. A central objective in LDC research is to rigorously characterize the optimal trade-off between code length and query complexity. Recently, [Y] introduced an innovative construction technique for LDCs that significantly improved upper bounds on code length by exploiting structural properties of Mersenne primes. Building upon this framework, we argue that further progress via these methods fundamentally depends on advances in a classical number-theoretic problem concerning the size of the largest prime factors of Mersenne numbers. Specifically, we demonstrate that for each Mersenne number \( m = 2^t - 1 \) possessing a prime factor \( p > m^\gamma \), one can construct a family of \( k(\gamma) \)-query LDCs whose length is bounded by \(\exp(n^{1/t})\). Conversely, if for some fixed \( k \) and every \( \epsilon > 0 \), the technique of [Y] yields a family of k-query LDCs with length \(\exp(n^\epsilon)\), then it necessarily follows that infinitely many Mersenne numbers have prime factors exceeding those currently known.

Reflectance, transmittance, and absorbance of a symmetric light pulse, whose carrier frequency closely matches that of interband transitions in a quantum well, are calculated. The quantum well is modeled with discrete energy levels, focusing on two closely spaced excited states. The analysis considers a wide quantum well whose width is comparable to the wavelength corresponding to the pulse’s carrier frequency, explicitly incorporating the dependence of the interband momentum operator matrix element on the light wave vector. Identical refractive indices are assumed for both the barriers and the quantum well. The problem is examined for an arbitrary ratio of radiative to nonradiative lifetimes of electronic excitations. The results demonstrate that spatial dispersion significantly influences the shapes of the reflected and transmitted pulses, with the most pronounced effects occurring when radiative broadening approaches the frequency difference between the two interband transitions under consideration.

The large-scale Galactic interstellar radiation field (ISRF) arises from stellar emission combined with subsequent reprocessing of starlight by interstellar dust. In regions of elevated ISRF energy density, such as the Galactic Centre, gamma-ray emission from individual supernova remnants (SNRs), including G0.9+0.1, predominantly results from inverse Compton (IC) scattering of ISRF photons. Several models have been developed to characterize the ISRF; notably, the most recent model produced by our group predicts a substantially higher ISRF intensity than the widely adopted model of Mathis, Mezger, and Panagia. However, empirical validation of these models remains limited to local observational data. Utilizing our current ISRF estimate, we forecast gamma-ray emission from the SNRs G0.9+0.1 and RXJ1713, as well as pair-production absorption features above 20 TeV in the spectra of G0.9+0.1, J1713-381, and J1634-472. Furthermore, we assess the capability of GLAST, in conjunction with existing and forthcoming very high energy instruments, to constrain the large-scale ISRF by establishing upper limits.

Bi-intuitionistic logic, an extension of intuitionistic logic incorporating a connective dual to implication, was originally formulated by Rauszer as a Hilbert calculus endowed with both algebraic and Kripke semantics. Despite this foundational framework, significant proof-theoretic challenges have emerged. Notably, Uustalu recently demonstrated that Rauszer’s subsequent “cut-free” sequent calculus for BiInt fails to satisfy the cut-elimination property. To remedy this deficiency, we introduce a novel cut-free sequent calculus for BiInt and rigorously establish its soundness and completeness with respect to Kripke semantics. The completeness proof is complicated by the intricate interaction between implication and its dual, a dynamic analogous to the interplay of future and past modalities in tense logic. Our calculus addresses this complexity by employing extended sequents that transmit information from premises to conclusions via variables instantiated at the leaves of failed derivation trees. Furthermore, a succinct termination argument enables the calculus to support automated deduction, although this is not its primary intended application.

We surveyed 2,772 2MASS/MSX/IRAS sources located off the Galactic plane (|b| > 3°) for the SiO J=1–0 v=1 and v=2 maser lines near 43 GHz, yielding 119 detections, 112 of which are previously unreported. Among these new detections are two exceptionally faint objects with MSX 12-micron flux densities below 2 Jy, likely O-rich AGB stars associated with dwarf galaxy tidal tails. The sample also comprises moderately bright MSX sources at intermediate Galactic latitudes (3° < |b| < 5°) and sources within the IRAS gap at higher latitudes. Analysis of a disk subsample reveals a warp in the inner Galactic disk, most prominent within 0° < l < 45° and 3° < |b| < 5°. Additionally, a stellar group near l ≈ 27° exhibiting kinematic deviations from standard Galactic rotation was identified; this structure extends over more than 15° in Galactic latitude and is consistent with a tidal debris stream originating from a dwarf galaxy.

This review examines the theory of dislocation motion within the periodic potential landscape of the crystal lattice, defined by the Peierls-Nabarro barriers. It first employs the kink mechanism to elucidate the temperature dependence of flow stress across a broad range of materials. The theory is subsequently extended to incorporate quantum mechanical dislocation tunneling through these barriers, supported by a rigorous comparison with experimental data on the plasticity of alkali halides and body-centered cubic (BCC) and hexagonal close-packed (HCP) metals at low temperatures. To model flow stress behavior in the regime exhibiting athermal anomalies, the dislocation motion mechanism is described as transitioning from thermally activated hopping to quantum tunneling through the barriers. Additionally, selected previously published results are reformulated into a more explicit, application-oriented format. Finally, the pronounced influence of the transition between normal and superconducting states on the flow stress of metals is interpreted through modifications in the dissipative properties of the electron subsystem, which critically govern dislocation dynamics.

The nonlinear kinetic theory of cosmic ray (CR) acceleration in supernova remnants (SNRs) is employed to calculate CR spectra, predicated on the substantial amplification of the magnetic field within SNRs by the efficient acceleration of nuclear CRs. The resulting spectra exhibit strong concordance with observational data up to energies of \(10^{17}\) eV. The proton spectrum follows a power-law distribution extending to approximately \(3 \times 10^{15}\) eV, beyond which it undergoes an exponential cutoff, thereby accounting for the observed knee in the Galactic CR spectrum. As the maximum energy attained by accelerated nuclei scales proportionally with their charge number \(Z\), the spectral break reflects the increasing predominance of heavier nuclei. Consequently, near \(10^{17}\) eV, the CR spectrum is dominated by iron group nuclei. Moreover, it is demonstrated that combining this heavy nuclei component with a suitably selected extragalactic CR component provides a consistent and comprehensive representation of the entire Galactic CR spectrum.

We estimate the bottomonium contribution to the electromagnetic current spectral function in hot QCD by applying the finite-temperature real-time static potential—recently derived to leading non-trivial order within Hard Thermal Loop resummed perturbation theory—and numerically solving the associated Schrödinger-type equation. The resulting spectral function displays a single resonance peak that broadens and ultimately vanishes as the temperature surpasses approximately 450 MeV. This thermal evolution contrasts with recent lattice reconstructions of the spectral function, obtained via the maximum entropy method, which typically reveal multiple resonance peaks. Additionally, we systematically examine the dependence of our results on both the spatial momentum of the electromagnetic current and the baryon chemical potential characterizing the hot QCD plasma.

Spectropolarimetric observations of neutral helium lines, particularly the 10830 Å multiplet, constitute a fundamental diagnostic for characterizing the magnetic properties of plasma structures in the solar chromosphere. In this context, we present a robust forward modeling and inversion code designed to (1) compute the emergent intensity and polarization for any specified magnetic field vector and (2) extract dynamical and magnetic parameters from the observed Stokes profiles. This diagnostic framework is firmly grounded in the quantum theory of spectral line polarization, which rigorously and self-consistently integrates both the Hanle and Zeeman effects within the comprehensive regime of the incomplete Paschen-Back effect. Furthermore, the code explicitly incorporates radiative transfer processes. To ensure computational efficiency and robustness, the methodology implements a numerical scheme based on global optimization techniques, enabling rapid and accurate convergence to the global minimum solution.

The multi-frequency Sedentary Survey constitutes a flux-limited, statistically robust sample of 150 BL Lacertae objects (HBLs) distinguished by pronounced X-ray dominance. This third paper in the series reports the results of a dedicated optical spectroscopy campaign which, combined with independent optical follow-up data, has enabled the complete spectroscopic identification of all sample sources. To this end, we systematically observed all previously unidentified objects using the ESO 3.6m, KPNO 4m, and TNG optical telescopes. Consequently, we present new identifications and optical spectra for 76 sources, comprising 50 newly identified BL Lacs, 18 previously classified BL Lacs lacking redshift determinations, and 8 broad emission line active galactic nuclei (AGNs). These findings confirm the high efficacy of the multi-frequency selection method, with approximately 90% of selected sources verified as BL Lacs. We provide positional and spectroscopic data for all confirmed BL Lacs. Redshifts were determined for 36 of the 50 new BL Lacs and 5 previously known objects. The redshift distribution of the complete sample is presented and compared with those of other BL Lac samples. For 26 sources without identifiable absorption features, lower redshift limits were derived using simulated optical spectra incorporating varying jet-to-galaxy emission ratios. Furthermore, within a subsample of 38 objects possessing high-quality spectra, we identify a correlation among optical spectral slope, 1.4 GHz radio luminosity, and Ca H&K break value, indicating that in powerful, beamed sources, optical emission is predominantly governed by non-thermal jet radiation.

A latin bitrade comprises a pair of disjoint partial latin squares occupying the same set of non-empty cells, with corresponding rows and columns containing identical sets of entries. Drápal (\cite{Dr9}) established that such a bitrade corresponds to a triple of derangements whose product equals the identity permutation, subject to the constraint that their cycles intersect pairwise in at most one point. By analyzing the action of a group on itself via right translation, we demonstrate that certain latin bitrades can be derived directly from groups without requiring an independent group action. Furthermore, fundamental structural properties of latin bitrades—namely homogeneity, minimality (captured by thinness), and orthogonality—are naturally encoded within this group-theoretic framework. Applying this construction to several well-known groups yields previously unknown latin bitrades. In particular, we prove the existence of minimal, \(k\)-homogeneous latin trades for every odd integer \(k \geq 3\), some of which represent the smallest known examples in this category.

Over the past three decades, research in nuclear physics and pulsar astrophysics has established that an elastodynamic framework within the continuum mechanics of nuclear matter accurately characterizes the macroscopic dynamics of degenerate Fermi matter constituting the interiors of nuclear material objects, the densest known structures to date. This paper addresses a specific theoretical facet of this development: the oscillatory behavior of a viscoelastic solid sphere undergoing quasistatic, force-free, non-compressional oscillations—a regime comparatively underexamined relative to oscillations involving standing shear waves. We demonstrate that, within this regime, the frequency and lifetime of spheroidal and torsional modes of non-radial shear vibrations damped by viscosity can be rigorously determined by applying the energy balance equation in conjunction with Rayleigh’s variational method. The applicability and robustness of this approach are exemplified through solid sphere models pertinent to nuclear physics and pulsar astrophysics, which analyze oscillations of a spherical viscoelastic Fermi-solid exhibiting both homogeneous and heterogeneous profiles of bulk density, shear modulus, and shear viscosity.

We present an automated method for parallelizing quantum circuits via forward and backward translations to measurement-based quantum computing patterns. Through a rigorous analysis of the trade-offs between circuit depth and space complexity, we identify a class of polynomial-depth circuits that can be transformed into logarithmic-depth circuits with only polynomial overhead in auxiliary qubits. Central to this approach is the first comprehensive characterization of patterns exhibiting flow of arbitrary depth, grounded in the concept of influencing paths and a concise rewriting system applied to measurement angles. This framework offers significant insights into the systematic design of parallel circuits. To demonstrate its practical applicability, we present several circuits achieving constant and logarithmic depth. Additionally, we establish a logarithmic separation in quantum depth between the quantum circuit model and the measurement-based quantum computing model.

Matter-light quantum interfaces and quantum memories for light constitute critical components of quantum information protocols, including quantum networks and distributed quantum computation. In this context, we present a spatially multimode quantum memory scheme for light, termed a quantum hologram. This scheme employs a multi-atom ensemble, previously demonstrated as effective for single spatial mode quantum memory. The multi-atom configuration inherently facilitates the simultaneous storage of multiple spatial modes, a capability central to the proposed approach. Compared to classical holograms, the quantum hologram offers superior storage capacity and faithfully preserves quantum properties of an image, such as multimode superpositions and entangled quantum states—features unattainable by conventional holograms. Moreover, by leveraging optical parallelism, the quantum hologram achieves an information capacity that significantly exceeds that of single-mode memory schemes.

Time series derived from commodity and asset prices have been systematically recorded and analyzed for several decades. Comprehensive documentation of every financial market transaction now generates a substantial dataset, accessible either freely via online platforms or through commercial providers. This extensive dataset has garnered significant interest from both practitioners and theoreticians, as the analysis of financial time series facilitates inference and predictive modeling. Moreover, the intrinsic stochastic uncertainties inherent in these series, combined with the requisite theoretical frameworks for their analysis, render this field particularly compelling to economists, statisticians, and physicists alike. While an exhaustive review of the subject would be a considerable undertaking, this article aims to provide a concise overview of its fundamental aspects.

Using the Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE), we observed the ultra-compact low-mass X-ray binary (LMXB) 1A 1246-588 and detected a kilohertz quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) exclusively during a soft, high-flux state analogous to the lower banana branch typical of atoll sources. This singular kilohertz QPO peak was identified at a frequency of 1258 ± 2 Hz, with a single-trial significance exceeding 7σ. Kilohertz QPOs at higher frequencies have been recorded only twice previously, both in 4U 0614+09. The observed frequency surpasses that of the lower kilohertz QPO in any known source, strongly indicating that the detected QPO corresponds to the upper peak of the kilohertz QPO pair commonly observed in LMXBs. The full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 25 ± 4 Hz yields the highest coherence reported for an upper kilohertz QPO. Based on a distance estimate of approximately 6 kpc from a radius expansion burst, we infer that 1A 1246-588 maintains a persistent flux of approximately 0.2–0.3% of the Eddington flux, placing it among the faintest LMXBs with a detected kilohertz QPO. The root-mean-square (rms) amplitude measured in the 5–60 keV energy band is 27 ± 3%, representing the highest rms amplitude recorded for any kilohertz QPO source to date. This observation aligns with the established anti-correlation between source luminosity and rms amplitude of the kilohertz QPO peak. Finally, analysis of a color-color diagram constructed from X-ray spectral data further substantiates the source’s classification as an atoll source.

Employing the one-dimensional Gross–Pitaevsky equation, we demonstrate the existence of waves localized at the interface between two nonlinear periodic media differing in cubic nonlinearity coefficients. These localized waves, termed surface gap solitons (SGSs), emerge under varying potential conditions. For smooth symmetric periodic potentials, we analytically examine SGS bifurcations originating from standard gap solitons and numerically determine the maximal permissible discontinuity in the nonlinearity coefficient that sustains SGS existence. Our results show that this maximal discontinuity diminishes to zero near the bifurcation thresholds of gap solitons. In the case of continuous potentials exhibiting a discontinuity in the first derivative at the interface, we develop a homotopy continuation method for SGS families, initiated from solutions formed by concatenating segments of standard gap solitons, to investigate SGS existence within photonic bandgaps. Furthermore, we establish that the termination of SGS families within band gaps corresponds to the bifurcation of linear bound states induced by the continuous non-smooth potentials.

We present a catalogue of morphologically classified bright galaxies within the north equatorial stripe (230 deg$^2$), compiled from the Third Data Release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). Morphological classification was conducted via visual inspection of $g$-band images. From an initial photometric sample of 2658 extended sources at a magnitude limit of $r=16$, corrected for Galactic extinction, we selected 2253 galaxies to constitute a complete catalogue. Spectroscopic data are available for 1866 of these galaxies. We provide a concise statistical analysis of the distribution of morphological types and mean colours. Additionally, visual inspection reveals that approximately 1.5% of galaxies within the $r \leq 16$ sample exhibit interaction features. Finally, we assess the completeness of the SDSS photometric catalogue, with particular emphasis on its bright-end accuracy.

We report preliminary results from two complementary blazar surveys directly relevant to GLAST detections of extragalactic sources, each employing a distinct selection strategy: microwave frequency selection and a combined deep X-ray/radio approach. The first survey comprises a 41 GHz flux-limited sample drawn from the WMAP three-year catalog of microwave point sources. This statistically robust sample includes approximately 200 blazars and radio galaxies, most of which are expected to be detected by GLAST. The second survey entails a deep examination of blazars identified among radio sources spatially coincident with serendipitous detections in deep X-ray observations (0.3–10 keV) centered on Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs) discovered by the Swift satellite. This sample is statistically significant because (a) it is unbiased, given the random sky distribution of GRBs; (b) it attains considerable depth in the X-ray band, reaching flux limits of \(\gtrsim 10^{-15}\) erg s\(^{-1}\) with positional accuracies of a few arcseconds; (c) it covers a sky area of 20–30 square degrees; (d) it encompasses all blazars with radio flux densities at 1.4 GHz exceeding 10 mJy, rendering it approximately two orders of magnitude deeper than the WMAP sample and roughly one order of magnitude deeper than the deepest existing complete radio-selected blazar samples; and (e) it facilitates estimation of the unresolved GLAST high-latitude gamma-ray background and its anisotropy spectrum. Collectively, these surveys establish a comprehensive framework for characterizing blazar populations pertinent to GLAST detections from both microwave and deep X-ray/radio perspectives.

Most information-theoretic inequalities follow from the fundamental properties of entropy or mutual information; however, Shannon's entropy power inequality (EPI) remains a notable exception. Existing proofs of the EPI represent differential entropy via Fisher information or minimum mean-square error (MMSE), both derived through de Bruijn's identity. This paper first establishes a unified framework for these proofs by identifying two key components: (1) a data processing argument applied to a covariance-preserving linear transformation, and (2) integration along a continuous Gaussian perturbation path. Building on these elements, we present a novel, concise proof of the EPI based on a mutual information inequality, supplanting the Fisher information inequality (FII) of Stam and Blachman and the MMSE inequality of Guo, Shamai, and Verdú employed in prior demonstrations. The principal advantage of this approach lies in its simplicity, as it depends solely on the fundamental properties of mutual information. We then extend these results to several generalizations of the EPI, including Zamir and Feder's generalized EPI for linear transformations of random variables, Takano and Johnson's EPI for dependent variables, Liu and Viswanath's covariance-constrained EPI, and Costa's concavity inequality for entropy power.

Lifshitz-type formulas are derived to quantify the free energy and force governing the van der Waals interaction between an atom (or molecule) and a single-wall carbon nanotube. In this formulation, the nanotube is modeled as a cylindrical sheet hosting a two-dimensional free electron gas, with appropriate boundary conditions imposed on the electromagnetic field. These formulas are subsequently employed to calculate the van der Waals free energy and force between a hydrogen atom (or molecule) and single-wall carbon nanotubes of varying radii. Comparative analyses of interactions involving hydrogen atoms and both single- and multi-wall carbon nanotubes demonstrate that, depending on the atom-nanotube separation distance, the approximation of graphite dielectric permittivity is applicable to nanotubes comprising only two or three walls.

Galaxy properties display a marked dependence on environment, with red galaxies predominantly located in clusters and blue galaxies more prevalent in the general field. Nonetheless, not all field galaxies are young. Comprehensive analyses of colors, spectral line strengths, and mass-to-light (M/L) ratios of massive early-type galaxies within 0 < z < 1.3 demonstrate that the most massive galaxies have comparable ages irrespective of environment, indicating largely environment-independent evolutionary trajectories. Furthermore, robust evidence indicates that the growth of these galaxies persists longer in the field than in clusters, primarily via (nearly) dissipationless mergers of pre-existing old galaxies. These findings are consistent with contemporary galaxy formation models incorporating active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback mechanisms that suppress star formation in the most massive halos.

Studies examining environmental effects beyond z = 1 remain methodologically challenging and yield somewhat inconsistent results. Both the DEEP2 and VVDS surveys report the disappearance of the color-density relation near z ≈ 1.3; however, this redshift corresponds to regions of significant incompleteness in both datasets. Conversely, clustering analyses at z ≈ 2.5 reveal stronger clustering of red galaxies relative to blue galaxies, indicating that the color-density relation was established by that epoch.

This paper examines several aspects of nonabelian gauged linear sigma models (GLSMs), beginning with a detailed review of their physical realization of partial flag manifolds, which generalize Grassmannians. This review emphasizes the construction of tangent bundles and other structures essential to (0,2) supersymmetric models. Building upon this foundation, we analyze the formation of Calabi–Yau complete intersections within these flag manifolds and investigate the resulting properties of the associated GLSMs. We then present multiple examples of nonabelian GLSMs whose Kähler phases are not related by birational equivalences, including cases where at least one phase is realized by mechanisms distinct from complete intersections, thereby extending prior work by Hori and Tong. Additionally, we examine an abelian GLSM exhibiting analogous phenomena. We propose that the mathematical correspondence underlying these non-birational phases can be interpreted as instances of Kuznetsov’s homological projective duality. Finally, we investigate the moduli spaces arising in these GLSMs, contending that the physically realized moduli spaces correspond precisely to Quot and hyperquot schemes, in accordance with established mathematical frameworks.

We present a mid-infrared (mid-IR) spectral decomposition of 48 Spitzer-selected ultraluminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs) spanning redshifts z ≈ 1–3, with infrared luminosities (L_IR) on the order of 10^12–10^13 L_⊙. This study quantitatively disentangles the relative contributions of star formation and active galactic nucleus (AGN) activity in these sources, which recent evidence indicates have undergone significant evolution since the observed epoch. To this end, we analyze mid-IR spectral components associated with polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) emission, continuum emission, and extinction.

Approximately 75% of the sample are dominated by continuum emission characteristic of AGN activity; notably, about 60% of these also exhibit PAH emission, indicating concurrent star formation. These sources display redder mid-IR colors relative to typical optically selected quasars. Conversely, roughly 25% exhibit strong PAH emission, yet none qualify as pure starbursts, as evidenced by their relatively elevated 5 μm hot dust continuum. Nonetheless, their steep flux ratios between 30 μm and 14 μm suggest that star formation may dominate their total infrared luminosity.

Within the z ~ 2 subset, six objects show equivalent widths of the 6.2 μm PAH feature (EW_6.2) ≥ 0.3 μm and 14 μm luminosities (L_14μm) near or exceeding 10^12 L_⊙, corresponding to total infrared luminosities (L_IR) of at least ~10^13 L_⊙. Such high EW_6.2 ULIRGs at these luminosities are absent in the local Universe. We measure a median optical depth at 9.7 μm of ⟨τ_9.7⟩ = 1.4, consistent with local IRAS-selected ULIRGs but divergent from earlier findings on SCUBA-selected z ~ 2 ULIRGs. Similar to local ULIRGs, approximately 25% of the sample exhibit extreme obscuration (τ_9.7 ≳ 3), indicative of deeply buried nuclei.

In summary, while our sample shares many characteristics with local ULIRGs, it is approximately an order of magnitude more luminous. Whether these z ~ 2 ULIRGs represent scaled-up analogs of local ULIRGs or are governed by fundamentally distinct physical mechanisms remains unresolved.

We report new results from our ongoing multiplicity survey of exoplanet host stars conducted with the SofI infrared camera at ESO-NTT, which has identified previously unrecognized low-mass companions to HD101930 and HD65216. The HD101930AB system is a wide binary comprising the primary star HD101930A and its companion HD101930B, classified as an M0 to M1 dwarf with an estimated mass of approximately 0.7 M☉, located at a projected separation of approximately 2200 AU (∼73 arcseconds).

In contrast, HD65216 is a hierarchical triple system. The planet host star HD65216A is separated by a projected distance of 253 AU (∼7 arcseconds) from the close binary companion HD65216BC, whose components are separated by approximately 0.17 arcseconds (6 AU). Proper motion analysis based on two VLT-NACO images obtained three years apart confirms that HD65216BC shares common motion with HD65216A, establishing their physical association. Infrared photometry classifies HD65216B as an M7 to M8 dwarf with a mass near 0.089 M☉, and HD65216C as an L2 to L3 dwarf with an estimated mass of 0.078 M☉; both lie near the sub-stellar boundary. Although the VLT-ISAAC infrared spectrum of HD65216BC is spatially unresolved, it substantiates this late spectral classification.

Additionally, we present H- and K-band ISAAC infrared spectra of HD16141B, a recently identified co-moving companion to the planet host star HD16141A. Both the infrared spectroscopic data and photometric analysis consistently indicate that HD16141B is an M2 to M3 dwarf located at the same distance as the primary star.

This paper presents a practical demonstration of assessing and propagating input uncertainty within tree-based option pricing models. It emphasizes that uncertainty in often unobservable input parameters systematically translates into uncertainty in option prices, thereby highlighting the fundamental indeterminacy inherent in these valuations. The validity of option pricing formulas depends not only on the model’s accuracy in capturing market dynamics but also critically on the quality of these latent input parameters. To address these challenges, we introduce three alternative calibration frameworks that explicitly incorporate parameter uncertainty into the resulting option prices. A comparative analysis of these frameworks against conventional calibration methods is then conducted, assuming the absence or illiquidity of an options market. These methodologies are applicable both to pricing instruments lacking an active options market and as robust tools for integrating parameter and model uncertainty within theoretical option pricing.

We analyze the satellite galaxy population generated in a series of N-body/gasdynamical simulations of galaxy formation within a ΛCDM cosmological framework. Our results reveal negligible spatial or kinematic bias between the satellite population and the dark matter distribution. Notably, the satellites’ velocity dispersion provides a reliable proxy for the halo’s virial velocity, quantified by the ratio \(\sigma_{\text{sat}} / V_{\text{vir}} = 0.9 \pm 0.2\). Applying this relation to the Milky Way and M31 yields virial velocities of \(109 \pm 22\) km/s and \(138 \pm 35\) km/s, respectively, both substantially lower than the rotation velocities of their disk components. Moreover, the detailed kinematic profiles of the simulated satellites closely correspond to those of the dark matter. In contrast, the stellar halo exhibits spatial and kinematic properties that differ markedly from those of the surviving satellite population. This disparity arises because satellite survival depends on both mass and accretion epoch; surviving satellites are predominantly lower-mass systems accreted more recently. Collectively, these findings support recent theoretical proposals attributing the systematic differences observed between stars in the Galactic halo and those in Galactic satellites to the progenitor “building blocks” of the Milky Way’s stellar halo, which were generally more massive and accreted and disrupted earlier than the dwarf galaxies that remain self-bound today.

Employing space velocities from the catalog of Nordstrom et al. (2004), we analyze the evolution of various kinematic parameters of single F and G dwarfs as functions of stellar age. Notably, the vertex deviation of disk stars increases from 7 ± 1° to 15 ± 2° as the mean age decreases from 4.3 to 1.5 Gyr. Examination of two-dimensional velocity distributions in the UV, UW, and VW planes enables tracking of principal peaks up to an average age of approximately 9 Gyr. The results indicate that stars of different types cluster around several stable peaks within the UV velocity distributions, corresponding to the Hyades, Pleiades, and Sirius Clusters, suggesting these groups’ constituent stars did not form contemporaneously. The Hyades Cluster peak consistently dominates all age intervals and attains maximal prominence among stars averaging 1.5 Gyr, indicating it contains a substantial fraction of stars originating from the Hyades cluster. Furthermore, the age dependence of kinematic parameters exhibits a discontinuity near 4.5 Gyr, reflecting varying contributions from the thin and thick Galactic disks. Application of the Stromberg relation yields a solar local standard of rest (LSR) velocity of V_{\odot LSR} = (8.7, 6.2, 7.2) ± (0.5, 2.2, 0.8) km/s.

We examine the orbital dynamics of satellite galaxies identified in a series of N-body/gasdynamical simulations modeling $L_*$ galaxy formation within a ΛCDM cosmological framework. The majority of satellites follow conventional trajectories: after turnaround, they accrete onto their host halo and settle into orbits whose apocentric radii progressively contract due to dynamical friction. However, approximately one-third of satellites at redshift $z=0$ exhibit apocenters exceeding their turnaround radii. This subset predominantly comprises the less luminous member of a satellite pair, dynamically ejected onto a highly energetic orbit during initial infall toward the primary galaxy. Given that simultaneous accretion of multiple satellite systems is a defining feature of hierarchical galaxy formation, we propose that this three-body ejection mechanism may account for (i) recently identified high-velocity satellites around M31, such as Andromeda XIV; (ii) distant, rapidly receding Local Group members including Leo I; and (iii) the anomalously isolated dwarf spheroidals Cetus and Tucana in the Local Group outskirts. These findings underscore the need for caution when using the orbital properties of the most weakly bound satellites to constrain the total mass of the Local Group.

We present recent findings on the magnetic and axial-vector transitions of the baryon antidecuplet within the chiral quark-soliton model, whose dynamical parameters are calibrated using experimental data on baryon octet magnetic moments, hyperon semileptonic decay constants, and the singlet axial-vector constant. This calibration permits accurate reproduction of the transition magnetic moments \(\mu_{\Lambda\Sigma}\) and \(\mu_{N\Delta}\) and enables predictions for additional octet-decuplet and octet-antidecuplet transitions. Significantly, the calculated value of \(\mu_{\Sigma\Sigma^*}\) remains below the recent upper bound of \(0.82 \mu_N\) established by the SELEX collaboration, providing a quantitative constraint consistent with experimental observations. Collectively, these results offer a coherent explanation for the newly observed \(N^*\) resonance reported by the GRAAL and Tohoku LNS collaborations. Furthermore, by determining the transition axial-vector constants for the \(\Theta^+ \to KN\) decay, we derive the \(\Theta^+\) pentaquark baryon decay width as a function of the pion-nucleon sigma term \(\Sigma_{\pi N}\). We also evaluate the sensitivity of this decay width to variations in the singlet axial-vector coupling \(g_A^{(0)}\) within its experimentally determined uncertainty range. Our analysis demonstrates that a narrow decay width \(\Gamma_{\Theta KN} \leq 1\) MeV for the \(\Theta^+ \to KN\) decay is consistent with established semileptonic decay data and the widely accepted proton value \(g_A^{(0)} \approx 0.3\).

We report the identification of the white dwarf/M dwarf binary system HS1857+5144 within the Hamburg Quasar Survey (HQS). To characterize this cataclysmic variable progenitor (pre-CV), we conducted time-resolved optical spectroscopy and photometry. The light curves exhibit sinusoidal variations with an orbital period (Porb) of 383.52 minutes and peak-to-peak amplitudes of 0.7 mag in the B-band and 1.1 mag in the R-band. This pronounced brightness modulation results from a reflection effect on the irradiated inner hemisphere of the companion star, indicating an exceptionally high white dwarf temperature. Radial velocity measurements confirm that the photometric period corresponds to the orbital period.

Model atmosphere fitting of the white dwarf spectrum at minimum light constrains its mass and temperature to approximately Mwd = 0.6–1.0 M⊙ and Twd = 70,000–100,000 K, respectively. The detection of He II 4686 absorption features classifies the primary as a DAO white dwarf. Integrating spectroscopic and photometric data, we estimate the companion star’s mass and the binary inclination to be Msec ≈ 0.15–0.30 M⊙ and i ≈ 45°–55°, respectively.

Accordingly, HS1857+5144 ranks among the youngest known pre-CVs. The white dwarf’s cooling age indicates that the system has recently emerged from a common envelope phase approximately 10^5 years ago. Furthermore, the system is predicted to initiate mass transfer within or below the 2–3 hour period gap.

We introduce a formal model for representing and solving unicast and multicast routing problems in networks constrained by Quality of Service (QoS) requirements. The method initiates by transforming the network into a weighted graph for unicast routing or an and-or graph for multicast routing. Within these graph structures, each connector’s weight represents the multidimensional cost of transmitting a packet over the corresponding network link, with each component of the weight vector corresponding to a distinct QoS metric (e.g., bandwidth, cost, delay, packet loss). This graph is subsequently encoded as a program within the Soft Constraint Logic Programming (SCLP) framework. Utilizing this encoding, the SCLP engine determines optimal paths or trees by minimizing costs while satisfying specified constraints (e.g., delay < 40 ms), thereby effectively addressing QoS routing challenges. Moreover, we underscore the appropriateness of c-semiring structures for modeling QoS metrics in this context. Finally, we present the implementation of the proposed model on scale-free networks and examine potential strategies for enhancing its performance.

Accepting the validity of Lorentz transformations for the space and time coordinates of a single event, we first derive their differential form to specify the exact conditions under which time and length contraction or dilation apply. We then quantify the simultaneity error intrinsic to relativity theory. This analysis reveals that these phenomena originate from a finite phase velocity associated with the moving frame, defined by analogy to the de Broglie wave of a moving particle. Within this framework, we demonstrate that the phase of de Broglie waves—including those corresponding to stationary particles—is a relativistic invariant, consistent across all corresponding observers. Similarly, the phase of electromagnetic waves, which mediate energy transport at light speed, also constitutes a relativistic invariant. Consequently, the universe and its matter-energy content can be interpreted as a superposition of waves propagating with a phase uniform for all corresponding observers. Thus, wave phase may serve as an invariant and universal reference, potentially supplanting time.

This study critically analyzes the mapping from time-dependent densities to potentials in quantum mechanics, a topic of enduring significance since Runge and Gross (Phys. Rev. Lett. 52, 997 (1984)) established its uniqueness, thereby laying the theoretical foundation for time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT). While existence (v-representability) and uniqueness criteria are well established, we contend that the stability and potential chaotic behavior of this mapping constitute equally essential considerations. Examination of a two-level system reveals seemingly innocuous, nearly constant densities that cannot be generated from any potential, demonstrating non-existence within this framework. Moreover, Lyapunov stability analysis uncovers chaotic regions in the density-to-potential mapping for this system. Extending to real space, despite the formal guarantee of v-representability, the mapping frequently exhibits chaotic dynamics that substantially impede the practical construction of the corresponding potential. The chaotic nature of this mapping, investigated here for the first time, has significant implications for the feasibility of employing TDDFT in real-time computational applications.

Color confinement and chiral symmetry constitute a fundamental theoretical framework in hadronic physics. Within this framework, hadrons are defined as color-singlet composite systems comprising quarks and gluons, the elementary fields of quantum chromodynamics (QCD). The hadronic spectrum is chiefly determined by the two light quark flavors, up (u) and down (d), whose masses are small relative to the intrinsic QCD scale. Observables sensitive to the orbital angular momentum of the nucleon’s color constituents provide critical insight into the interplay between chiral symmetry and confinement. This interplay can be rigorously analyzed via the Georgi-Manohar chiral quark model, which facilitates the evaluation of the renormalization of orbital structure functions alongside the normalization of Boer-Mulders functions across quark flavors. The resulting resolution structures correspond to calculations of Collins functions for a confined system characterized by the nucleon’s quantum numbers within the constituent quark model. Additionally, orbital structure functions for antiquarks can be consistently formulated within this framework, whereas normalizing the gluon orbital structure function requires supplementary assumptions.

The stability of two-dimensional (2D) layers and membranes has long constituted a central focus of theoretical investigation. The Mermin-Wagner theorem demonstrates that long-wavelength fluctuations disrupt long-range order in 2D crystals. Analogously, 2D membranes embedded within three-dimensional (3D) space are prone to crumpling induced by such fluctuations. Nonetheless, anharmonic coupling between bending and stretching modes counteracts these destabilizing effects, enabling the existence of 2D membranes characterized by pronounced height fluctuations. The discovery of graphene—the first unequivocal 2D crystal—and the recent experimental observation of ripples in freely suspended graphene underscore the critical importance of these phenomena. Beyond their theoretical relevance, elucidating the mechanisms underpinning graphene’s stability is essential for understanding its electronic transport properties, distinguished by an unusual Dirac spectrum and unique electronic behavior. In this study, we investigate graphene’s height fluctuations via atomistic Monte Carlo simulations employing a highly accurate many-body interatomic potential for carbon. Our results reveal that ripples spontaneously emerge from thermal fluctuations, exhibiting a size distribution peaked near 70 Å. This finding aligns with experimental measurements (50–100 Å) yet challenges prevailing theoretical models of flexible membrane stability. We ascribe this anomalous behavior to the multiplicity of chemical bonding configurations inherent to carbon.

This paper extends the theory of filtration-consistent nonlinear expectations (or "${\cal F}$-consistent nonlinear expectations") to settings dominated by a $g$-expectation potentially exhibiting quadratic growth. Within this framework, we demonstrate the preservation of fundamental martingale properties, including the Doob-Meyer type decomposition theorem and the optional sampling theorem. Central to our results is the proof that any quadratic ${\cal F}$-consistent nonlinear expectation satisfying a specified domination condition coincides with a quadratic $g$-expectation. The principal contribution is the identification of a novel domination condition that supplants the previously employed condition, which fails in the quadratic context. Moreover, we establish that the associated representation generator is necessarily deterministic, continuous, and assumes a particularly simple form.

This study examines the development of anomalous film thickness features in elastohydrodynamic contacts lubricated with fatty alcohol. Experiments utilizing a ball-on-disk apparatus systematically varied the slide-to-roll ratio between a steel ball and a glass disk. Lauric alcohol was employed as the lubricant, and film thickness within the contact region was measured via optical interferometry. Under pure rolling conditions, the film thickness distribution conformed to the classical profile; however, increasing the slide-to-roll ratio induced significant alterations in film morphology. In particular, the central contact zone thickness increased, accompanied by modifications in both the inlet and outlet film thicknesses. Furthermore, film shapes varied depending on whether the ball surface moved faster than the disk or vice versa, despite slide-to-roll ratios being equal in magnitude but opposite in sign.

A definitive demonstration has confirmed that the shear-thinning behavior influencing both film thickness and traction in elastohydrodynamic lubrication (EHL) contacts conforms to the classical power-law relationship described by several empirical models, including the Carreau model. This conclusion was established by integrating precise viscometric measurements of the shear response of a polyalphaolefin (PAO) fluid—characterized by an exceptionally low critical stress threshold for shear-thinning—with accurate in-contact measurements of film thickness and traction obtained under conditions emphasizing the shear-thinning effect. Employing straightforward computational methods based on rheological properties derived from viscometry, central film thickness and traction were predicted with high accuracy. These findings offer valuable insights for researchers seeking to simulate Hertzian contact behavior with high fidelity, supported by comprehensive characterization of shear-thinning rheology and robust in-contact validation data. Furthermore, a novel model has been introduced to advance the rheological characterization of fluid mixtures.

Building on the seminal experimental studies of superlubricity by Martin et al. on MoS2 [1], Hirano et al. on tungsten and silicon [2], and the subsequent validation by Dienwiebel et al. on graphite [3], numerous research groups worldwide have investigated near-frictionless sliding contacts. This extensive interdisciplinary collaboration among tribologists, materials scientists, and physicists has facilitated the development of novel materials and coatings, with carbon-based substances—including graphite, diamond, carbon composites, and diamond-like carbons—emerging as the most promising candidates. Several of these materials have already been implemented in practical applications.
