These experimental findings are corroborated by first-principles band-structure calculations that provide a microscopic elucidation of the underlying structural and magnetic phenomena.

We investigate the energetically lowest-lying states in the BEC-BCS crossover regime of harmonically confined s-wave interacting two-component Fermi gases by solving the many-body Schrödinger equation through two complementary methodologies. For systems with \(N=4\) fermions, we employ essentially exact basis set expansion techniques to accurately resolve the energy spectrum. For larger systems containing up to \(N=20\) fermions, we apply fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo methods, accompanied by a detailed analysis of the guiding functions used to enforce the required fermionic symmetry. Energies are computed as functions of the s-wave scattering length \(a_s\) for particle numbers ranging from \(N=2\) to 20 and various mass ratios \(\kappa\) between the species. In both the BEC and BCS regimes, these results align with analytically derived first-order correction terms. From these calculations, we extract the scattering length and effective range characterizing the dimer-dimer system for mass ratios up to \(\kappa=20\). At unitarity, the strongly interacting trapped system exhibits no shell structure, and its energy spectra are well described by a simple expression derived from the local density approximation involving one or two parameters. Finally, we determine the universal parameter \(\xi\) for the trapped system across different \(\kappa\) values and compare these findings with corresponding results for the homogeneous system.

We present a novel spinfoam vertex for four-dimensional quantum gravity models based on SU(2) and SO(4) BF theory with supplementary constraints. Reformulated within a basis constructed from SU(2) coherent states, this vertex corresponds to the conventional SU(2) BF theory vertex represented by the 15j symbol. This basis affords a transparent geometric interpretation of the variables as vectors normal to the triangles within each tetrahedron. We analyze the conditions under which these states qualify as semiclassical and demonstrate that such states predominantly govern the evaluation of quantum correlations. Finally, we express the constraints reducing BF theory to gravity directly in terms of these variables and discuss how the semiclassical character of the states may enhance the precise implementation of these constraints.

This study presents a novel examination of the small-scale dynamics of turbulent flow lacking strong mean shear within a Newtonian fluid near the turbulent/non-turbulent interface. It employs two principal methodologies: three-dimensional particle tracking velocimetry (3D-PTV) for Lagrangian measurement and tracking of the velocity gradient tensor, and direct numerical simulations (DNS). Through systematic comparison of flow properties across three contiguous regions—turbulent (A), intermediate (B), and non-turbulent (C)—the investigation elucidates the fundamental physical mechanisms underlying entrainment. Crucially, the pronounced disparities observed between small-scale strain and enstrophy reinforce a framework in which turbulent entrainment is predominantly governed by viscous forces arising from strain.

The Positive Mass Conjecture states that any complete asymptotically flat manifold with nonnegative scalar curvature necessarily has nonnegative mass and further requires that if the mass vanishes, the manifold is isometric to Euclidean space. This conjecture was proven by R. Schoen and S.-T. Yau for manifolds of dimension less than eight and independently by E. Witten for all spin manifolds. In this paper, we investigate complete asymptotically flat manifolds with nonnegative scalar curvature that are additionally harmonically flat at an end. Assuming the validity of the Positive Mass Theorem, we establish that any suitably normalized sequence of such manifolds with masses converging to zero admits metrics converging uniformly to the Euclidean metric outside a compact set. This convergence result constitutes a fundamental component of a forthcoming joint proof with H. Bray of the Riemannian Penrose inequality in dimensions less than eight.

This study rigorously examines two-qubit entanglement within the most general XYZ Heisenberg spin chain by integrating uniform and nonuniform magnetic fields with the Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya (DM) anisotropic antisymmetric exchange interaction derived from spin–orbit coupling. By subsuming the well-established XX, XY, XXX, XXZ, and XYZ chains across both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic regimes as limiting cases, the model provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing thermal entanglement. We systematically investigate the concurrence of two-qubit thermal states, elucidating its dependence on anisotropy parameters, external magnetic field intensities, and temperature. Our results consistently demonstrate that inclusion of the DM interaction—known to induce weak ferromagnetism in predominantly antiferromagnetic crystals and to modulate spin configurations in low-symmetry magnets—either generates entanglement when absent or enhances it when present in the XYZ chain. This finding underscores a fundamental linkage between spin arrangement and entanglement mediated by DM coupling and establishes the anisotropic antisymmetric exchange interaction as an effective control parameter for tuning entanglement in the general XYZ model.

Employing the Jaynes-Cummings model within the rotating-wave approximation, we investigate the entanglement conditions of a system comprising two atoms interacting with two photon modes in vacuum. Building on prior research, we demonstrate that the entanglement strength exhibits periodic temporal behavior and explicitly verify that our results converge to established conditions under suitable limiting cases. We then extend the analysis to arbitrary atomic energies corresponding to photon mode frequencies, thereby advancing previous work through a unified treatment of both resonant and nonresonant regimes. Our findings reveal that entanglement periodicity is an inherent feature of the resonant regime. Focusing on the two-atom, two-photon configuration, we develop a framework generalizable to many-particle systems, facilitating a comprehensive examination of the resulting master equation.

Galaxy-scale gravitational lenses are routinely modeled by combining a universal dark matter density profile exhibiting ellipsoidal symmetry with a Sersic profile characterizing the baryonic matter distribution. Accurate prediction of lensing phenomena thus necessitates comprehensive characterization of the total lens potential. To this end, we present analytic expressions for the lens potential of this composite model. Exploiting the principle that complex lens potentials can be synthesized through linear combinations of simpler components, we introduce a systematic method to impose elliptical symmetry on either the projected mass distribution or directly on the lens potential. Additionally, we derive analytic formulae for the lens potentials of Sersic profiles with both integer and half-integer indices.

Building on this foundation, we develop expressions for gravitational lensing effects induced by smoothly truncated universal density profiles within the cold dark matter paradigm. Specifically, in isolated halos, the density profile declines beyond the tidal radius following a power law proportional to the radius raised to the negative fifth or seventh power. These functional forms enable analytic computation of lens potential derivatives to all orders while ensuring a finite total mass. We further clarify how lensing observables predicted by this truncated profile diverge from those associated with the original infinite-mass Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) profile, with particular emphasis on gravitational flexion.

Furthermore, we demonstrate that reducing the tidal radius facilitates modeling of stripped halos, thereby establishing a robust framework for detailed investigations of dark matter substructure within galaxies and clusters. Finally, we emphasize the necessity of employing finite-mass halo profiles in cosmological ray-tracing simulations and underscore the critical importance of readily computable higher-order derivatives of the lens potential for effective analysis of catastrophes in strong lensing phenomena.

Integrated experimental and theoretical methodologies were employed to investigate the conformational dynamics of giant DNA in bulk solutions containing condensing agents. Experimentally, pronounced hysteresis was observed during folding and unfolding transitions, corresponding to systematic increases and subsequent decreases in polyethylene glycol (PEG) concentration. To elucidate the mechanism underlying this hysteresis, Monte Carlo simulations were conducted on a semiflexible chain model undergoing the coil–globule transition. These simulations demonstrate that hysteresis loops arise exclusively in sufficiently stiff chains, reflecting distinct folding and unfolding pathways. Moreover, within these loops, the globular state is thermodynamically favored over the coiled state. Collectively, these findings indicate that increased chain stiffness restricts the conformational space accessible during folding, thereby impeding the folding process.

We report three years of timing observations of PSR J1453+1902, a 5.79-ms pulsar identified in a 430-MHz drift-scan survey conducted with the Arecibo telescope. Our data confirm that PSR J1453+1902 is isolated and exhibits a proper motion of 8(2) mas yr⁻¹. Combining this measurement with the nominal distance of 1.2 kpc inferred from its dispersion measure yields a transverse velocity of 46(11) km s⁻¹, consistent with typical velocities observed among millisecond pulsars. To assess potential luminosity differences between isolated and binary systems, we analyze a sample of 55 millisecond pulsars in the Galactic disk. We demonstrate that the apparent disparities in luminosity distributions derived from 430-MHz survey samples can be attributed to small-number statistics and observational selection biases. Furthermore, analysis of 1400-MHz survey samples reveals no statistically significant luminosity differences between these groups. Accordingly, the most parsimonious interpretation supported by the current data is that isolated and binary millisecond pulsars exhibit consistent spin, kinematic, spatial, and luminosity properties, indicative of a single, homogeneous population.

Investigating particle production mechanisms in hadronic collisions necessitates a sensitive experimental methodology involving measurements of diverse particle species across an extended momentum range. Utilizing data acquired with the STAR detector at RHIC, analyses of spectral shapes as a function of collision centrality elucidate the interplay between soft and hard meson production processes and enable detailed examination of specific baryon-meson phenomena. Furthermore, systematic analyses of identified particle spectra across various colliding systems and incident energies provide critical insights into the relative contributions of fragmentation and non-fragmentation mechanisms. Within this context, we present a comprehensive study of transverse momentum spectra for charged pions, protons, and antiprotons produced in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at √s_NN = 200 and 62.4 GeV, evaluated according to collision centrality. These findings are subsequently compared with corresponding data from p+p and d+Au collisions to assess the influence of system size on partonic energy loss.

This work builds upon the analyses in \cite{li-qva1} and \cite{li-qva2}, which examine vertex algebra-like structures arising from various algebraic frameworks, including quantum affine algebras and Yangians. Specifically, we investigate two variants of the double Yangian $DY_{\hbar}(sl_{2})$, namely $DY_{q}(sl_{2})$ and $DY_{q}^{\infty}(sl_{2})$, where $q$ is a nonzero complex parameter. For each such $q$, we construct a quantum vertex algebra $V_{q}$ and demonstrate that every $DY_{q}(sl_{2})$-module naturally inherits a $V_{q}$-module structure. Conversely, we characterize $DY_{q}^{\infty}(sl_{2})$-modules as $V_{q}$-modules-at-infinity.

To elucidate these correspondences, we introduce the notions of $\mathcal{S}$-local and quasi-local subsets within $\Hom(W, W((x^{-1})))$ for an arbitrary vector space $W$. We prove that any $\mathcal{S}$-local subset generates a (weak) quantum vertex algebra, while any quasi-local subset generates a vertex algebra in which $W$ functions as a (left) quasi module-at-infinity. This framework further facilitates the connection between the Lie algebra of pseudo-differential operators on the circle and vertex algebras, realized through the construction of quasi modules-at-infinity.

The resonant bar detector network for gravitational waves within the International Gravitational Event Collaboration (IGEC-2) comprises four instruments: ALLEGRO, AURIGA, EXPLORER, and NAUTILUS. This report details the outcomes of a six-month search for gravitational wave bursts conducted in 2005, during which IGEC-2 served as the sole active gravitational wave observatory. The data analysis prioritized time coincidence searches among AURIGA, EXPLORER, and NAUTILUS, reserving ALLEGRO data for subsequent follow-up investigations. Compared to IGEC observations from 1997 to 2000, the detectors demonstrated approximately a threefold improvement in amplitude sensitivity to bursts, alongside an expanded sensitivity bandwidth. These enhancements necessitated refinement of the analysis to encompass a broader range of detectable waveforms. Moreover, improved duty cycles of the individual detectors enabled a focus on three-fold coincidence events, thereby ensuring reliable identification of any gravitational wave candidate with high statistical confidence. Consequently, the false alarm rate was reduced to as low as one per century. Ultimately, no gravitational wave candidates were identified.

The dynamic properties of molecular motors, which generate motion through active interactions with underlying molecular tracks, are theoretically investigated using discrete-state stochastic "burnt-bridge" models. In this framework, particle transport is modeled as effective diffusion along one-dimensional lattices with periodically spaced weak links. Upon traversing a weak link, an unbiased random walker may irreversibly destroy ("burn") it with probability p, thereby inducing a directional bias in the motor’s movement. We develop a theoretical framework that enables the exact determination of all dynamic properties of motor proteins, including velocity and dispersion, under general conditions. Our analysis reveals that dispersion decreases as the concentration of weak links increases, while its dependence on the burning probability exhibits a more complex pattern. Furthermore, the calculations identify a discontinuity in dispersion at very low weak link concentrations, indicating a dynamic phase transition between unbiased and biased diffusion regimes. These theoretical predictions are corroborated by Monte Carlo simulations.

This study presents a rigorous analysis of the twist-2 and twist-3 light-cone distribution amplitudes (LCDAs) for the $1^3P_1$ and $1^1P_1$ axial-vector mesons within the QCD conformal partial wave expansion framework. Through systematic decomposition of the twist-three two-parton LCDAs into leading-twist and twist-three three-parton LCDAs via the equations of motion, a hierarchical structure elucidating their interdependencies is established. Employing the QCD sum rule method, G-parity invariant and violating parameters—including corrections from SU(3) symmetry breaking—are extracted. The results comprise axial-vector decay constants for the $1^3P_1$ states, alongside updated tensor decay constants and Gegenbauer moments characterizing the leading-twist distribution amplitudes of the $1^1P_1$ states. Application of the Gell-Mann–Okubo mass formula yields mixing angles of approximately $\theta_{^3P_1} \sim 38^\circ$ for the $f_8$ and $f_1$ components of the $1^3P_1$ states, and $\theta_{^1P_1} \sim 10^\circ$ for the $h_8$ and $h_1$ components of the $1^1P_1$ states, thereby clarifying their flavor composition. Detailed characterizations of the physical states $f_1(1285)$, $f_1(1420)$, $h_1(1170)$, and $h_1(1380)$ further inform their phenomenological profiles. Assuming a mixing angle $\theta_K = \pm 45^\circ$ between $K_{1A}$ and $K_{1B}$, the analysis is extended to the $K_1(1270)$ and $K_1(1400)$ states. Finally, models for the LCDAs are constructed via the conformal partial wave expansion, incorporating terms up to conformal spin 9/2 to capture higher-order effects. Notably, certain distribution amplitudes exhibit significant asymmetry, which may have important implications for phenomenological applications.

Bluffing, owing to its intricate and contested nature, persistently challenges game designers and thereby impedes the development of intelligent virtual players capable of realistic gameplay. By integrating intelligent learning agents with meticulously designed perspectives, an agent can anticipate opponents’ reactions through systematic evaluation of both its own cards and the behaviors of other players. This enhanced situational awareness enables the agent to employ bluffing as a deliberate strategic behavior aimed at maximizing returns via rigorous statistical optimization rather than as an irrational act. Through iterative refinement of neural network-based agent intelligence using a TD(lambda) learning algorithm, these systems have demonstrated the capacity to autonomously acquire bluffing proficiency and to detect and call opponents’ bluffs during free, competitive play.

The \(n\)-dimensional complex hyperquadric, defined as a compact complex algebraic hypersurface by a quadratic equation in \((n+1)\)-dimensional complex projective space, is isometric to the real Grassmann manifold of oriented 2-planes and constitutes a compact Hermitian symmetric space of rank 2. This study applies the framework of isoparametric hypersurfaces in spheres to analyze the geometry of compact Lagrangian submanifolds within complex hyperquadrics. Through this approach, we establish a classification theorem for compact homogeneous Lagrangian submanifolds using the moment map technique. Additionally, we examine the Hamiltonian stability of compact minimal Lagrangian submanifolds embedded in complex hyperquadrics, focusing on those realized as Gauss images of isoparametric hypersurfaces in spheres with \(g = 1, 2, 3\) distinct principal curvatures.

We systematically examine the effects of variations in fundamental couplings and mass scales on primordial nucleosynthesis. The analysis commences with an evaluation of elemental abundance sensitivities to perturbations across a broad range of nuclear physics parameters, emphasizing nuclear binding energies. This evaluation demonstrates that the neutron–proton mass difference predominantly governs the ^4He yield, the nucleon mass critically influences deuterium production, and the binding energies of nuclei with mass numbers A = 3, 4, and 7 substantially regulate the abundances of ^3He, ^6Li, and ^7Li. Building upon these findings, we establish explicit correspondences between these nuclear parameters and the fundamental constants of the Standard Model. Notably, the abundances of deuterium and especially ^7Li exhibit pronounced sensitivity to the average light quark mass \(\hat{m} \equiv (m_u + m_d)/2\). We then compute the shifts in elemental yields induced by variations in fundamental parameters constrained by grand unification relations. Finally, we assess the potential for a significant alteration in the lithium abundance while the abundances of deuterium and ^4He remain comparatively stable.

High-mass star formation remains poorly understood, primarily because high-mass young stellar objects (YSOs) are typically distant, deeply embedded, and often indistinguishable from other emission sources. These factors have significantly constrained dynamical investigations at spatial scales of tens of astronomical units (AU), which are critical for examining the regions where accretion disk outflows are launched and collimated. To address these limitations, the KaLYPSO project utilizes SiO maser observations from the Very Large Array (VLA) and the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) to characterize the structural, dynamical, and temporal evolution of material between 10 and 1000 AU from the nearest high-mass YSO, Radio Source I, in the Orion BN/KL region. The dataset comprises approximately 40 VLBA epochs collected over several years, enabling precise tracking of individual SiO maser spot proper motions and monitoring temporal variations in the physical conditions of the emitting material. Ultimately, these observations will facilitate the construction of three-dimensional maps of the outflow structure spanning approximately 30% of the outflow crossing time. Here, we summarize recent findings from the KaLYPSO project, which provide compelling evidence that high-mass star formation proceeds via disk-mediated accretion.

We present optical photometry and optical-to-mid-infrared spectroscopy of the classical nova V1186 Sco, which exhibited a slowly evolving, complex light curve marked by multiple secondary peaks analogous to those observed in PW Vul. Although the two-magnitude decline time (t$_2$) was measured at 20 days, the pronounced variability of the light curve undermines reliable determination of intrinsic properties, such as luminosity, based on this metric. Consequently, the widely employed maximum magnitude–rate of decline (MMRD) relation of Della Valle and Livio (1995) fails to provide a credible distance estimate.

Spectroscopic observations spanning 0.35 to 35 μm were obtained at two epochs within the first year post-outburst. Approximately two months after visible maximum, the initial spectra display features characteristic of a CO-type nova, including narrow emission lines of \ion{H}{1}, \ion{Fe}{2}, \ion{O}{1}, and \ion{He}{1}. Subsequent observations between 260 and 380 days post-maximum reveal the emergence of a nebular spectrum. During this phase, *Spitzer* spectra exhibit diminished hydrogen recombination emission concurrent with the appearance of [\ion{Ne}{2}] (12.81 μm) as the dominant emission line, accompanied by significant detection of [\ion{Ne}{3}] (15.56 μm).

Photoionization modeling incorporating low effective temperature sources and marginal neon enrichment (Ne ≈ 1.3 Ne$_{\odot}$) successfully reproduces the observed infrared fine-structure neon lines, indicating that V1186 Sco did not originate from an ONeMg white dwarf. Rather, the integrated evidence from the slow, irregular light curve evolution, spectral progression, and photoionization analysis collectively supports an outburst on a low-mass CO white dwarf. Notably, this study reports the earliest detection of strong [\ion{Ne}{2}] lines in a CO nova outburst, demonstrating that mid-infrared neon lines are not exclusive diagnostic indicators of ONeMg nova events.

We present a high-resolution X-ray imaging analysis of the stellar population within the Galactic massive star-forming region RCW49 and its central OB association, Westerlund 2. This study employed a 40 ks exposure from the Chandra X-ray Observatory covering a 17′ × 17′ field, supplemented by deep near-infrared (NIR) imaging from the Infrared Survey Facility over a concentric 8.3′ × 8.3′ area. A total of 468 X-ray sources were detected, with 379 matched to optical, NIR, and Spitzer Space Telescope mid-infrared (MIR) counterparts. Integrating the high spatial resolution and sensitivity of the X-ray data with multiwavelength observations, we derived the following principal findings:

(1) Westerlund 2 is spatially resolved in the X-ray band for the first time, with emission detected from all spectroscopically confirmed early-type stars, thereby confirming their X-ray activity.

(2) Comparison with a Galactic Plane control field indicates that 86% of X-ray sources exhibiting optical or infrared counterparts are bona fide cluster members, effectively delineating the association’s stellar population.

(3) A distance estimate of 2–5 kpc for RCW49 is derived from the mean X-ray luminosity of T Tauri stars, consistent with prior determinations.

(4) The cluster’s X-ray population comprises both low-mass pre–main-sequence and early-type stars, identified through combined X-ray and NIR photometry; this analysis also facilitated the identification of approximately 30 newly recognized OB star candidates.

(5) Analysis of X-ray surface number density profiles yields an estimated cluster radius of approximately 6′–7′, delineating the spatial extent of the association.

(6) Approximately 90% of cluster members are individually identified through complementary X-ray detections and MIR excess emission, underscoring the efficacy of multiwavelength diagnostics for membership confirmation.

(7) The five most luminous X-ray sources—two Wolf-Rayet stars and three O-type stars—exhibit hard thermal spectra, indicative of their energetic stellar environments and associated high-energy emission processes.

Within an effective framework characterizing active-sterile neutrino mixing in a thermally equilibrated medium, we investigate sterile species production by deriving the quantum kinetic equations governing both distribution functions and coherences. These equations are obtained through two independent methodologies: the effective action and the quantum master equation. The decoherence time scale for active-sterile oscillations is defined as \(\tau_{dec} = 2/\Gamma_{aa}\), where \(\Gamma_{aa}\) denotes the interaction rate of the active species absent mixing. In contrast, the temporal evolution of the distribution functions is dictated by two distinct damping rates of quasiparticle modes, \(\Gamma_1 = \Gamma_{aa} \cos^2 \theta_m\) and \(\Gamma_2 = \Gamma_{aa} \sin^2 \theta_m\), with \(\theta_m\) representing the mixing angle in the medium. This pronounced disparity between time scales, particularly away from MSW resonances, precludes a kinetic description of active-sterile production via a simple rate equation. We provide a comprehensive set of quantum kinetic equations describing the active and sterile populations and their coherences, accompanied by a detailed analysis of various approximations. Furthermore, we generalize the active-sterile transition probability within the medium by employing the quantum master equation. Finally, we explicitly derive the conventional quantum kinetic equations expressed in terms of the “polarization vector” and establish their equivalence to those obtained from both the quantum master equation and the effective action.

Prochter et al. (2006) reported that the number density of strong intervening MgII absorbers detected in gamma-ray burst (GRB) afterglow spectra at redshifts 0.5 < z < 2 exceeds that observed in quasar (QSO) spectra by nearly a factor of four. To further examine this disparity, we conducted a comparable study targeting CIV absorbers. Our sample comprises 20 CIV systems identified from three high-resolution, high to moderate signal-to-noise VLT/UVES spectra of long-duration GRB afterglows, spanning the redshift range 1.6 < z < 3.1. Comparative analysis of the column density and number density distributions reveals no statistically significant differences relative to QSO measurements. After evaluating several potential explanations for the divergent behaviors of CIV and MgII absorbers, we conclude that increased dust extinction in the MgII QSO samples studied to date offers the most straightforward explanation, although this effect primarily impacts strong MgII absorbers. Regardless of the underlying cause, our findings reaffirm the utility of GRBs as probes of previously inaccessible regions of the universe—regions not necessarily associated with the GRBs themselves—thus providing an alternative and indispensable tool for investigating cosmic evolution.

A survey of Galactic gamma-ray sources at a median energy near 20 TeV was conducted using the Milagro Gamma Ray Observatory, encompassing the Galactic longitude interval \( l \in [30^\circ, 220^\circ] \) and latitude interval \( b \in [-10^\circ, 10^\circ] \). This study identified eight candidate TeV emission sources with pre-trials significances exceeding \(4.5\sigma\). Following correction for multiple trials across the 3800 square degree survey area, four sources—including the Crab Nebula and the recently reported MGRO J2019+37—retained significances above \(4\sigma\); all four are spatially coincident with EGRET detections. Among the remaining lower-significance candidates, two also correspond to EGRET sources, one being Geminga, while the other two are situated within the Cygnus region. Several sources exhibit spatial extension, with measured fluxes at 20 TeV ranging from approximately 25% to nearly 100% of the Crab flux.

The expansion of ionization fronts within uniform, spherically symmetric power-law density distributions has been extensively investigated. However, in various astrophysical contexts—such as star formation at the periphery of a molecular cloud core—an offset power-law density distribution provides a more accurate environmental characterization. This study examines the formation and expansion of HII regions in such offset media, with particular emphasis on density profiles proportional to 1/r² and 1/r³. To assess whether the initial photoionized region remains bounded, a criterion is established based on the power-law exponent and the ratio of the equivalent Stroemgren radius (computed for a uniform medium) to the stellar offset distance. During the subsequent expansion phase, the ionized volume will ultimately become unbounded unless pressure equilibrium with the external medium is attained before the ionization front velocity exceeds the sound speed within the ionized gas.

We propose a model based on the symmetry group SU(5) × {}^{(d)}T that simultaneously accounts for near tri-bimaximal leptonic mixing and realistic CKM matrix elements for quarks. This framework successfully reproduces the Georgi-Jarlskog relations across all three generations. A pivotal aspect of the model is the specific {}^{(d)}T transformation properties assigned to the matter fields, which cause the b-quark mass to arise exclusively upon breaking the {}^{(d)}T symmetry; this mechanism thus provides a dynamical explanation for the mass hierarchy between \(m_b\) and \(m_t\). Furthermore, the inclusion of an additional \(Z_{12} \times Z'_{12}\) symmetry restricts the Yukawa sector to nine operators up to at least mass dimension seven and effectively suppresses, to high orders, operators capable of inducing proton decay. Consequently, the model involves nine parameters within the charged fermion and neutrino sectors, thereby enhancing its predictive power. Notably, it predicts \(\theta_{13} \simeq \theta_c / (3 \sqrt{2})\) and establishes the sum rule \(\tan^{2} \theta_{\odot} \simeq \tan^{2} \theta_{\odot, \mathrm{TBM}} - \frac{1}{2} \theta_c \cos \beta\). This sum rule, derived from the Georgi-Jarlskog relations in the quark sector, compellingly explains the discrepancy between the experimentally favored solar mixing angle and that predicted by the tri-bimaximal mixing matrix.

The prevailing model for long-duration gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) ascribes their origin to the collapse of a massive star into a black hole, occurring via direct collapse or fallback accretion. When formation proceeds through fallback, radioactive nickel synthesis is markedly suppressed, prompting the hypothesis—albeit without rigorous computational validation—that these events produce intrinsically faint supernovae. Recently, such fallback black-hole GRBs have been identified as progenitors of a newly recognized subclass of GRBs lacking associated supernova emission. Here, we present the first radiation-hydrodynamics simulations of the light curves generated by the hypernova explosion accompanying a delayed-fallback GRB. Our findings demonstrate that the bolometric light curve is predominantly driven by shock-deposited energy rather than radioactive decay. Consequently, observations of these bursts primarily constrain the density structure of the progenitor’s circumstellar wind rather than the mass of synthesized radioactive nickel.

We investigate a diffusion model incorporating limit cycle reaction functions under convection, employing functions derived from the Schnakenberg reaction model. Despite the system’s intrinsic asymmetry, we identify a transformation that recasts the irregular equations into a canonical form. To facilitate travelling wave analysis centered on the radial component, the dependent variables are expressed in polar coordinates. Although the resulting dynamics are complex, several concise estimates are derived. To validate these theoretical predictions, numerical simulations are conducted wherein pattern propagation is initiated by an initial perturbation (“knock”). The observed travelling wave speed deviates from initial expectations, necessitating further analysis. Notably, the system exhibits markedly distinct behaviors on the left and right sides, a phenomenon elucidated through comprehensive examination of the underlying dynamics.

We present refined quantum Monte Carlo estimators for the spherically- and system-averaged electron pair density—defined as the probability density of finding two electrons separated by a relative distance u and commonly denoted as the spherically-averaged electron position intracule density I(u). This advancement builds upon the general zero-variance zero-bias principle for observables formulated by Assaraf and Caffarel. The evaluation of I(u) is significantly enhanced by substituting the average of the local delta-function operator with that of a smooth non-local operator, achieving a variance reduction of several orders of magnitude. This substitution improves computational efficiency and markedly reduces the systematic error (bias) associated with approximate trial wave functions. When combined with the systematic optimization of an increasing number of parameters in trial Jastrow-Slater wave functions, the methodology enables accurate and well-converged determination of correlated intracule densities for atoms and molecules. Moreover, the approach readily generalizes to the computation of arbitrary pair-correlation functions within both classical and quantum Monte Carlo frameworks.

B-band light-curve rise times for eight exceptionally well-observed nearby Type Ia supernovae (SNe) were analyzed using a novel template-building algorithm that generates smooth and flexible light-curve functions, thereby mitigating biases associated with externally derived templates or prior assumptions. Photometric BVRI data, collected over several months and including the earliest observations, were systematically reconciled, consolidated, and fitted to establish a precise explosion epoch for each SN. After correction for light-curve decline rate, three SNe exhibited a mean rise time of 18.81 ± 0.36 days, while five exhibited a mean rise time of 16.64 ± 0.21 days. Although statistical analyses do not support the hypothesis that all eight SNe originate from a single parent population, adopting this assumption enables the first quantification of the root-mean-square intrinsic scatter in the decline-rate-corrected rise time, measured as 0.96^{+0.52}_{-0.25} days. The corresponding global mean rise time, predominantly influenced by intrinsic variance, is 17.44 ± 0.39 days—approximately two days shorter than two previously published averages, which, despite claiming nominally twice the precision, are also based on limited samples. In the context of comparing high- and low-redshift SN luminosities for cosmological parameter estimation, employing a light-curve template with an inaccurate rise time can introduce systematic bias. Specifically, when the temporal coverage of light-curve sampling varies with redshift, as is typical in current observational protocols, a two-day discrepancy in template rise time can bias luminosity comparisons by approximately 0.03 magnitudes.

In several physically significant contexts, exact solutions to the Einstein equations with nonhomogeneous (anisotropic) cosmological constants effectively model nonholonomically (nonintegrable) constrained Ricci flows. To construct these solutions, we introduce two geometric methodologies. The first employs the formalism of nonholonomic frame deformations, which reformulates the gravitational evolution and field equations into systems of nonlinear partial differential equations integrable in general form. The second establishes a comprehensive framework that generates one- or two-parameter families of exact solutions derived from source-free solutions of Einstein’s equations possessing one or two Killing vector fields, respectively. By implementing a successive iteration procedure, this framework yields a class of solutions characterized by infinitely many parameters associated with a non-Abelian group defined by arbitrary functions of a single variable. Additionally, we examine nonlinear superpositions of selected solution classes to construct more general integral varieties of the Ricci flow and Einstein equations. These solutions depend on infinitely many parameters and three or four coordinates within four- or five-dimensional (semi) Riemannian manifolds.

This study examines Ricci flows of physically significant solutions in Einstein and string gravity by employing the anholonomic frame method applied to a generic off-diagonal metric ansatz, thereby reformulating the field and evolution equations as exactly integrable systems of partial differential equations. The resulting solution families, constructed within four- and five-dimensional gravitational frameworks, depend on arbitrary generation and integration functions of one to three variables. Imposing specific nonholonomic frame constraints enables the isolation of vacuum and/or Einstein metrics, while further generalizations incorporate nontrivial string sources—such as antisymmetric torsion fields—and matter contributions. A defining feature of this methodology, originally developed in Finsler and Lagrange geometry and subsequently adapted to semi-Riemannian spaces, is its capacity to generate novel exact solutions via nonholonomic deformations parameterized by generalized Geroch transforms and Ricci flow evolution parameters. In this work, we explicitly construct multiple classes of exact solutions for multi-parameter Einstein spaces and their associated nonholonomic Ricci flows, which characterize the evolution and interaction of solitonic pp-waves alongside deformations of the Schwarzschild metric. Finally, we evaluate the potential physical implications of these solutions and their significance within contemporary gravitational theory.

The function exp(iωt) characterizes oscillatory motion, with the oscillator’s energy proportional to the square of the angular frequency ω. It satisfies a differential equation that is subsequently reformulated as an equivalent finite-time difference equation, where d denotes the minimal time interval. To preserve invariance under the transformation d → −d, this difference equation is symmetrized. This symmetrization yields paired solutions modifying ω to either ω′ or ω″; ω′ incorporates an integer component, whereas ω″ comprises a half-integer component, reflecting the quantized energy levels characteristic of quantum mechanical oscillators. The function F = a·exp(iωt) describes oscillations confined within the bounds of −a and +a; setting ω to zero yields free oscillations within the same amplitude range. Consequently, the reciprocal symmetric oscillator framework unifies the descriptions of quantum and classical harmonic oscillators, as well as those of a harmonic oscillator and a free particle confined within a potential well, without invoking quantum mechanical postulates.

We theoretically demonstrate the emergence of multiple bi-stability regions within the temperature profile at the interface of a cuprous oxide quantum well and the organic compound DCM2:CA:PS. This phenomenon derives from CA-induced solvatochromism, which precisely tunes the Frenkel molecular exciton of DCM2 into resonance with the $1S$ quadrupole Wannier-Mott exciton in cuprous oxide, thereby generating a hybrid exciton state. Subsequent thermalization of this hybrid exciton via interaction with the surrounding helium bath induces a pronounced nonlinear temperature dependence of the laser field detuning relative to the quadrupole exciton energy band. This nonlinearity originates from the temperature-driven red shift of the Wannier exciton energy. Numerical simulations incorporating both upward and downward detuning scans reveal a hysteresis-like temperature distribution. Notably, the multiple bi-stability regions identified exceed previously observed bi-stability in bulk cuprous oxide by at least three orders of magnitude (meV scale versus μeV scale). Furthermore, the effective absorption spectrum exhibits marked asymmetry between the Frenkel-like branch, positioned above the $1S$ energy, and the Wannier-like branch, positioned below it.

Semiring-based constraint satisfaction problems (semiring CSPs), as introduced by Bistarelli, Montanari, and Rossi \cite{BMR97}, constitute a broadly applicable framework for modeling soft constraints. This paper develops an abstraction scheme that rigorously formalizes the correspondence between abstract and concrete problem instances via semiring homomorphisms. The approach begins by solving the abstract problem to identify its optimal solutions, which subsequently guide the solution of the corresponding concrete problem. We prove that a mapping preserves optimal solutions if and only if it is an order-reflecting semiring homomorphism. Moreover, given a semiring homomorphism \(\alpha\) and a problem \(P\) defined over a semiring \(S\), if \(t\) is an optimal solution to the abstract problem \(\alpha(P)\), then there exists an optimal solution \(\bar{t}\) to the original problem \(P\) such that \(\bar{t}\) attains the same value as \(t\) under \(\alpha(P)\).

This work advances the theory developed in [Ca01] = math.AG/0110051 by introducing the bimeromorphic *category* of geometric orbifolds, which serve as intermediaries between compact Kähler manifolds and those endowed with logarithmic structures. We examine geometric orbifolds through their intrinsic geometry, equipping them with classical invariants traditionally associated with varieties—such as morphisms and bimeromorphic maps, differential forms, fundamental groups and universal covers, fields of definition, and rational points. In this paper, we establish the foundational properties of geometric orbifolds by directly adapting results from the theory of varieties without orbifold structures. This foundational framework facilitates a direct extension of the arguments in [Ca01], thereby yielding the principal structural results within this orbifold category. More advanced topics will be addressed in subsequent work.

The impetus for this framework stems from the recognition that the natural setting for the classification theory of compact Kähler and complex projective manifolds necessarily encompasses the category of orbifolds. This is exemplified in [Ca01] by the functorial decomposition of *special* manifolds into towers of orbifolds characterized by either \(\kappa_+ = -\infty\) or \(\kappa = 0\), a perspective further corroborated by the minimal model program, wherein many proofs require the inclusion of a "boundary." Moreover, fibrations within the bimeromorphic category of geometric orbifolds exhibit extension properties absent in the category of varieties without orbifold structures. These properties permit expressing invariants of the total space in terms of those of the generic fiber and the base. For example, the natural sequence of fundamental groups is exact in this context, and the total space is special whenever both the generic fiber and the base are special. Accordingly, this category provides a natural and effective framework for transferring properties from orbifolds with either \(\kappa_+ = -\infty\) or \(\kappa = 0\) to those classified as special.

This paper presents the design of a mechanical transmission incorporating a comprehensive analysis of transmitted forces. The design centers on the Slide-o-Cam mechanism, comprising multiple rollers mounted on a common translating follower. As previously documented, the Slide-o-Cam facilitates bidirectional conversion between rotational input and sliding motion. By enabling pure rolling contact, this mechanism significantly reduces the frictional losses typically observed in rack-and-pinion and linear drive systems. A critical performance parameter, the pressure angle, governs the distribution of force between the load and the machine frame. To rigorously evaluate load-bearing capacity, Hertz contact theory is applied to quantify stresses on both rollers and cams. This transmission is intended to replace existing ball-screw assemblies in the Orthoglide, a three-degree-of-freedom parallel robot currently under development at Ecole Centrale de Nantes for machining applications requiring precise translational motion.

This study examines the interaction between a particle’s electric and magnetic dipole moments and the electromagnetic field within a framework based on four-dimensional (4D) geometric quantities. Within this context, novel commutation relations are formulated for the 4D orbital and intrinsic angular momenta, as well as for the 4D dipole moments. These relations enable the derivation of the expectation value of the quantum 4-force, which is shown to be invariant across all inertial reference frames. In contrast, the analysis in [1] (J. Anandan, Phys. Rev. Lett. 85, 1354 (2000)) is limited to the dipole’s rest frame. Moreover, it is demonstrated that, for example, the three-dimensional force \(\mathbf{f}_S\) presented in [1] lacks relativistic consistency and that the quantum 4-force remains nonzero in the proposed experimental setups. Therefore, the phase shifts observed in these experiments cannot be interpreted as topological phase shifts.

We reexamine trans-Planckian corrections to inflationary spectra by incorporating a previously neglected physical effect with potentially significant implications. We posit that the short length scale characterizing the new physics—likely originating from quantum gravity—possesses a finite width, inducing a blurring of the ultraviolet (UV) scale. This blurring typically attenuates the leading corrections responsible for superimposed oscillations in the CMB temperature anisotropies. To evaluate the observational implications of this attenuation, we compare it with the damping inherent in the computation of the angular power spectrum of temperature anisotropies. While attenuation due to the finite width results in an overall reduction of oscillation amplitudes, the damping in the angular power spectrum varies with angular scale. This distinction suggests that, in principle, these effects could be observationally distinguished. In any event, the detection of superimposed oscillations would impose stringent constraints on the variance of the UV cutoff.

The potential existence of intermediate-mass black holes within globular cluster cores has attracted considerable scholarly attention. Previous theoretical and simulation-based studies have identified an enlarged core radius—or more specifically, an elevated core-to-half-mass radius ratio—as a reliable indicator of such black holes in star clusters. To evaluate this hypothesis, the present study employs N-body simulations of 100,000 stars, incorporating scenarios both with and without primordial binaries, to examine the long-term structural evolution of star clusters. Importantly, the simulation outputs are analyzed using methodologies identical to those applied in observational studies to derive structural parameters, thereby facilitating direct comparison of core-to-half-mass (or half-light) radius ratios with those observed in the Galactic globular cluster population. The results demonstrate that most observed ratios can be explained without invoking intermediate-mass black holes. Moreover, clusters exhibiting large core-to-half-light radius ratios may instead host black-hole binary systems composed of stellar-mass black holes rather than a single massive black hole. Nonetheless, this study does not preclude the existence of intermediate-mass black holes in the cores of certain star clusters.

Building on the eleven-dimensional \(E_{11}\) non-linear realisation of M-theory, we systematically classify all forms—entities defined by fully antisymmetrised indices—that arise in four or more dimensions, as well as all 1-forms and 2-forms in three dimensions. In any dimension \(D\), the \((D-1)\)-forms generate maximal supergravity theories incorporating cosmological constants, precisely reflecting the gauging patterns established via supersymmetry. The \(D\)-forms correspond to space-filling branes, which are essential for maintaining the consistency of orientifold models; notably, these branes have been derived through alternative methods exclusively in the ten-dimensional setting. Accordingly, both the gaugings of supergravity theories and the spacetime-filling branes originate within the eleven-dimensional \(E_{11}\) framework of M-theory. Together with preceding results, these findings compellingly substantiate the physical interpretation of all fields residing in the adjoint representation of \(E_{11}\).

We rigorously analyze transcritical bifurcations of periodic orbits in non-integrable two-dimensional Hamiltonian systems by employing a recently developed mathematical framework for transcritical bifurcations in families of symplectic maps. This framework enables a comprehensive investigation of their existence criteria and intrinsic properties. Building on this foundation, we present numerical examples from a class of generalized Hénon-Heiles Hamiltonians that elucidate the stability characteristics and unfolding dynamics of these bifurcations under various Hamiltonian perturbations. Our findings establish that transcritical bifurcations of straight-line librating orbits constitute the generic scenario within such Hamiltonians, occurring even in the absence of discrete symmetries; in contrast, isochronous pitchfork bifurcations arise as exceptional phenomena. Furthermore, we derive the normal forms associated with both bifurcation types and develop the uniform approximation necessary to incorporate transcritically bifurcating orbits into the semiclassical trace formula for the density of states of the corresponding quantum Hamiltonian. Finally, semiclassical and quantum mechanical computations of the coarse-grained density of states for a representative example demonstrate excellent concordance between the two methodologies.

In the 1980s, Stallings demonstrated that every finitely generated subgroup of a free group admits a canonical representation as a finite minimal immersion of a bouquet of circles. Interpreted through automata theory, this topological representation corresponds to a minimal finite inverse automaton, thereby enabling the application of the algorithmic frameworks of finite automata and finite inverse monoids to problems concerning such subgroups. This study aims to extend these methods to a broader class of groups. A central challenge in this extension is the modification of the Stallings folding algorithm to accommodate the "sewing" of relations inherent to non-free groups. We focus on groups constructed as amalgams of finite groups, which are known to be locally quasiconvex; this property ensures that all finitely generated subgroups admit finite automaton representations. We propose an algorithm for constructing these automata and demonstrate its efficacy in resolving various algorithmic problems.

We present a solution to the equivalence problem in three-dimensional gravity, along with a practical method for obtaining a coordinate-invariant characterization of local geometry. This method constitutes a nontrivial adaptation of Karlhede’s invariant classification scheme, originally developed for spacetimes in general relativity. The local geometric structure is completely determined by the curvature tensor and a finite sequence of its covariant derivatives, each evaluated within a frame where the metric components remain constant. Employing the formalism of real two-component spinors in three-dimensional spacetimes, we provide algebraic classifications of the Ricci and Cotton-York spinors and identify their associated isotropy groups and canonical forms. Utilizing this framework, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for local spatial and temporal homogeneity in Gödel-type spacetimes within three-dimensional general relativity. Additionally, we analyze the equivalence classes of these spacetimes and critically compare our findings with previous studies of four-dimensional Gödel-type spacetimes.

Max-product belief propagation is a local, iterative algorithm devised to compute the mode or MAP estimate of a probability distribution. Despite its broad applicability, theoretical guarantees of convergence and correctness for general loopy graphs—particularly those with numerous short cycles—remain limited, with exact necessary and sufficient conditions notably rare. This study examines the application of max-product to identify the maximum weight matching in arbitrary graphs with weighted edges. To this end, we first construct a probability distribution whose mode corresponds exactly to the optimal matching, then apply max-product to this distribution. Alternatively, the weighted matching problem can be formulated as an integer program with an associated linear programming (LP) relaxation, which is not invariably tight. We establish two principal results: (1) when the LP relaxation is tight, max-product consistently converges to the correct solution; and (2) when the LP relaxation is loose, max-product fails to converge. These findings provide an exact, data-dependent characterization of max-product’s behavior and rigorously connect its performance to LP relaxation, a well-established optimization framework. Moreover, since LP relaxation is known to be tight for bipartite graphs, our results extend and generalize recent advances in applying max-product to weighted matchings within bipartite graphs.

Astronomical spectrographs typically achieve resolutions ranging from several hundred to 200,000. Calibration of low- and high-resolution spectroscopy predominantly depends on HeAr and ThAr lamps, respectively. However, these lamps emit spectral lines confined to a limited segment of the spectrometer’s range, with line wavelengths exhibiting marked sensitivity to environmental fluctuations. Furthermore, line intensities vary significantly, with ratios exceeding 300. This limited and inconsistent luminosity further compromises their efficacy in illuminating spectrographs via integrating spheres, a technique critical for ensuring uniform illumination of long-slit spectrograph pupils during calibration.

In contrast, laboratory precision laser spectroscopy has progressed substantially through the development of optical frequency combs generated by pulsed femtosecond lasers. These lasers produce a broad spectrum extending several hundred nanometers across the visible and near-infrared regions, comprising equally spaced “comb” lines with near-uniform intensities, typically characterized by intensity ratios below 10. Their intrinsic self-referencing mechanism establishes an exceptionally precise frequency standard, facilitating stabilization to an uncertainty of 10⁻¹⁸ and achieving absolute frequency inaccuracies on the order of 10⁻¹² per day when calibrated against the Global Positioning System (GPS) time signal. Consequently, this technology offers considerable promise for providing broadband, highly accurate, and reproducible calibration—imperative for the reliable operation of current and next-generation astronomical spectrometers.

This study develops a systematic framework for closing overdetermined systems derived from conformal Killing tensors (CKTs), with particular emphasis on 1-tensors and 2-tensors. The proposed methodology establishes a generalizable approach applicable to CKTs of arbitrary rank and naturally extends to other classes of Killing equations, as well as to overdetermined systems subject to additional constraints.

Central to this framework is the decomposition of the section bundles containing the covariant derivatives of CKTs via generalized gradients. This decomposition arranges the derivatives into a hierarchical tree structure, wherein each level corresponds to derivatives of progressively higher order. Imposing the conformal Killing equation eliminates the majority of components, leaving only a subset expressible in terms of lower-order terms. This reduction yields a finite set of independent jets, thereby enabling the representation of any higher-order covariant derivative through these jets.

The findings bear substantial methodological significance and contribute to advancing the identification of symmetries. Specifically, the study introduces a novel procedure for closing overdetermined systems associated with CKTs. Application of this procedure recovers first- and second-degree higher-order symmetry operators for the Laplace operator, thus corroborating prior results obtained through alternative methods. Additionally, it identifies first-order symmetry operators for the Yamabe operator and formulates conjectures regarding its second-order symmetries.

This project evaluated the one-loop fermion self-energy for massless Dirac fermions coupled to Einstein gravity in a locally de Sitter background. By systematically applying dimensional regularization, all divergences were absorbed via Bogoliubov-Parasiuk-Hepp-Zimmermann (BPHZ) counterterms, yielding a fully renormalized expression. A key technical challenge arose from the breaking of de Sitter invariance induced by the selected gauge condition, necessitating the introduction of a noninvariant counterterm. Furthermore, the effective Dirac equation for massless fermions during inflation was solved in the simplest gauge, incorporating all one-loop quantum gravity corrections. At late times, the spatial plane wave solution exhibits behavior analogous to a classical solution undergoing time-dependent field strength renormalization, expressed as \( Z_2(t) = 1 - \frac{17}{4\pi} G H^2 \ln(a) + O(G^2) \). This behavior similarly emerges within the Hartree approximation, albeit with differing numerical coefficients.

We present numerical simulations of stellar wind dynamics within the central parsec of the Galactic Centre, focusing on gas accretion onto Sgr A*, the supermassive black hole. Unlike prior studies, these simulations incorporate the latest observational data on the orbits and wind properties of individual wind-producing stars. The integration of revised, elevated wind velocities with non-zero stellar eccentricities reduces the frequency of cold gas clumps and suppresses the formation of a distinct disc-like structure. Accretion is primarily governed by a limited subset of proximate "slow wind stars" with wind velocities v_w < 750 km/s and aligns with the Bondi accretion rate; nevertheless, it exhibits variability over timescales of tens to hundreds of years. This variability arises from both the stochastic infall of cold gas clumps, consistent with earlier simulations, and the dynamical influence of stellar eccentricities. Although the current models do not reproduce the enhanced luminosity of Sgr A* inferred from Integral observations several hundred years ago, we propose that accretion of a cold clump with a small impact parameter may account for this phenomenon. Finally, we demonstrate that near-infrared observations of gas within the central few arcseconds provide a viable method to constrain the total mass-loss rate of the slow wind stars.

This study rigorously assesses the influence of Pauli non-locality within the heavy-ion optical potential on sub-barrier fusion reactions. The S\~{a}o Paulo potential, which explicitly incorporates Pauli non-locality and has been extensively applied in elastic scattering analyses, has recently been extended to heavy-ion fusion. However, as its derivation is based on the Perey-Buck semi-classical method originally developed for neutron-induced reactions, a comprehensive evaluation of its suitability for modeling charged-particle tunneling through a potential barrier is necessary. To this end, we examine the well-characterized system $^{16}$O + $^{208}$Pb across an energy range spanning 10 MeV below to 10 MeV above the fusion barrier. Our findings indicate that within this interval, the effect of non-locality is minimal and that the S\~{a}o Paulo potential provides an adequately accurate description throughout the evaluated domain.

Classical and quantum phase transitions are characterized by observables exhibiting non-analytic behavior as functions of a controlled thermodynamic variable. The emergence of such discontinuities fundamentally depends on the precise evaluation of the classical or quantum thermodynamic limit, as exemplified by the self-consistent Fermi Golden Rule. Within this framework, we demonstrate that a quantum two-level system coupled to an environment—whose oscillatory dynamics resemble those of a classical damped oscillator—undergoes a quantum dynamical phase transition from an oscillatory to a non-oscillatory regime. This transition results from a self-consistent solution of the Generalized Landauer-Büttiker Equations, which offer a simplified integral formulation of the Keldysh formalism. We further contend that the system’s behavior on either side of this transition corresponds to fundamentally distinct paradigms in the Kuhnian sense. Consequently, the incommensurability of these paradigms is rigorously justified as a direct mathematical outcome of the observables’ non-analyticity. Moreover, we emphasize the critical importance of cultivating public intuition and understanding concerning the abrupt shift from static to dynamical friction regimes.

Keywords: Self-Consistent Fermi Golden Rule, Paradigm Shift, Quantum Dynamical Phase Transition, Decoherence, Energy-Time Wigner Function, Dissipative Two-Level System, Keldysh Formalism, Generalized Landauer-Büttiker Equations, Loschmidt Echo, Mesoscopic Echo, Spin Dynamics, Solid State NMR, Dynamical Quantum Zeno Effect, Liquid Crystal NMR.

This paper examines the stability of selected ideal stars within the framework of General Relativity, focusing on the interaction between matter and gravitational fields to enhance understanding of strong gravitational regimes and Black Holes. The analysis is grounded in an action principle governing the coupled metric and matter fields. We present a comprehensive revision of the conventional treatment of boundary conditions. An ideal star is defined as a spherically symmetric object obeying an isentropic equation of state. Although our initial study assumed that density vanishes beyond a finite radius, difficulties in specifying appropriate boundary conditions challenge the validity of imposing a fixed boundary. To address this issue, we analyze the double polytrope model, characterized by a polytropic index \( n < 5 \) within the stellar interior and exceeding 5 in an outer atmosphere extending to infinity. Unlike fixed-boundary models, this approach incorporates a critical density region where the polytropic index transitions from the interior value to one approximating the atmospheric region. Our findings confirm the existence of a mass-radius relation and an upper mass limit. The principal conclusion is that all static configurations considered are stable.

Database search, a fundamental subroutine in numerous critical algorithms, has broad applicability. This study examines a database containing a single target item, which quantum algorithms identify more efficiently than any classical counterpart. In many practical scenarios, however, the objective extends beyond precisely locating the target item to retrieving a subset of information related to it or identifying a collection of items sharing a common attribute with the target. Consequently, the problem is reformulated as a search for a segment of the database—a block—that contains the target item rather than the item itself. This method, termed partial search, sacrifices exactness to achieve enhanced performance relative to a full search.

Originally introduced by Grover and Radhakrishnan, the partial search algorithm is analyzed here in an optimized variant designated GRK. This algorithm can be applied iteratively: first, the database is partitioned into blocks, enabling GRK to identify the target block; then, this block is further subdivided into sub-blocks, and GRK is reapplied to locate the target sub-block. This iterative procedure is known as binary quantum search. Alternatively, the database may be partitioned directly into sub-blocks, allowing GRK to locate the target sub-block in a single application. We demonstrate that this latter approach is more efficient, requiring fewer queries to the oracle.

Many natural systems—including glasses, interfaces, and fractures—fail to equilibrate with their environment, resulting in emergent phenomena such as memory effects, ageing, and nonlinear dynamics. Unlike equilibrated systems, the dynamics of these out-of-equilibrium systems are typically too complex to be captured by simple macroscopic laws. This study examines a system situated at the boundary between glassy and crystalline phases: a Bragg glass composed of vortices in a superconductor. The system’s response to an externally applied force follows a stretched exponential function, with the exponent quantifying the extent of deviation from equilibrium. Upon removal of the force, the system undergoes ageing, characterized by a response time that scales linearly with its chronological age—a phenomenon termed simple ageing—which indicates that older systems respond more slowly than younger ones. We further demonstrate that simple ageing arises inherently in the presence of sufficient quenched disorder. Moreover, the observed stretched-exponential response originates from a hierarchical distribution of timescales, resulting from the immobilization of loosely bound vortices until trapped vortices are released.

We conduct chemodynamical simulations to assess the impact of stellar winds from massive stars on the early dynamical and chemical evolution of nascent globular clusters (GCs). In these models, GCs form within turbulent, high-density giant molecular clouds (GMCs) embedded in massive dark matter halos at high redshifts. The formation of dense, compact stellar systems arises from the interaction between star formation processes within GMCs and the tidal forces exerted by their host halos. Chemical enrichment of these GC-forming GMCs by massive-star winds results in star-to-star variations in light-element abundances—specifically carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen—among GC stars. Employing a canonical initial mass function (IMF), the simulations reproduce a characteristic C–N anticorrelation, whereby stars with lower [C/Fe] ratios correspondingly exhibit higher [N/Fe]. Although these findings support the hypothesis that “self-pollution” by massive-star winds induces abundance inhomogeneities, models with varied parameters and canonical IMFs fail to replicate the extremely nitrogen-rich stars ([N/Fe] ≈ 0.8) observed in certain GCs, such as NGC 6752. This limitation is interpreted within the framework of a “bimodal star formation scenario,” which posits that massive star formation precedes low-mass star formation within GC-forming GMCs. Furthermore, while the majority of stars (~97%) display typical helium abundances (Y ≈ 0.24), a minor fraction formed during later evolutionary stages of GMCs attain helium mass fractions up to ~0.3 in some models. Nonetheless, the proportion of helium-enhanced stars with Y > 0.26 remains exceedingly low (~10⁻³) across most simulations.

We present spectroscopic observations of 11 moderately high-redshift clusters (z ~ 0.7–1.0) from the first Red-Sequence Cluster Survey (RCS-1). For clusters with z > 0.7, red-sequence estimated redshifts closely correspond to spectroscopic measurements, exhibiting an approximate scatter of 10%. At the upper redshift limit of the sample (z ≳ 0.9), two systems are identified as projections of pairs of comparably rich clusters whose red sequences are indistinguishable in (R–z′) color, complicating their separation. In one case, the close spatial proximity of these components suggests a probable physical association. Examining a subset of clusters with sufficient spectroscopic membership, we investigate the relationship between optical richness, quantified by B_gcR, and dynamical mass inferred from velocity dispersion measurements. Despite substantial uncertainties, our findings align with the correlation previously established at lower redshift for both the X-ray selected CNOC1 clusters and a lower redshift RCS-1 sample. Definitive confirmation of this correlation and precise calibration of its scatter will require larger cluster samples encompassing these and higher redshift regimes.

This paper examines energy efficiency in wireless data networks through a game-theoretic framework wherein each user strategically optimizes transmit power, spreading code, and uplink receiver configuration to maximize utility, defined as the ratio of data throughput to transmit power. The analysis initially addresses receivers employing linear multiuser detectors before extending to the more intricate scenario involving non-linear decision feedback multiuser receivers. In both cases, the utility maximization problem is formulated as a non-cooperative game, with the existence of a unique Nash equilibrium rigorously established. Simulation results demonstrate that substantial performance gains are obtained through both non-linear processing and spreading code optimization. Specifically, spreading code optimization yields the most pronounced improvements when the number of users does not exceed the processing gain, whereas non-linear processing provides the greatest enhancements in overloaded systems. Across all scenarios, the proposed non-cooperative game framework consistently outperforms alternative methodologies.

The Navier-Stokes equations within a finite cylinder are rigorously formulated using poloidal and toroidal potentials to enforce incompressibility. To ensure solution regularity, a systematic approach is adopted. Initially, the potentials are expanded in a spectral basis that preserves analyticity at the cylindrical axis. Subsequently, non-physical discontinuous boundary conditions at the cylindrical corners are smoothed by approximating a steep exponential profile with a polynomial function. Finally, the nonlinear term is evaluated via a technique specifically designed to eliminate singularities. The resulting pseudo-spectral code is validated against exact polynomial solutions, confirming spectral convergence of the expansion coefficients. The computed solutions exhibit strong concordance with these exact solutions, as well as with prior axisymmetric simulations of vortex breakdown and nonaxisymmetric analyses of helical spiral onset. Moreover, parallelization with respect to the azimuthal wavenumber achieves high computational efficiency.

This paper investigates the perturbative properties of a "B-twisted" two-dimensional $(0,2)$ heterotic sigma model formulated on a holomorphic gauge bundle $\mathcal{E}$ over a complex Hermitian manifold $X$. We demonstrate that this model is naturally embedded within the mathematical framework of Chiral Differential Operators (CDO), within which the physical anomalies appear as obstructions to the global definition of the associated sheaf of vertex superalgebras, locally arising from the free conformal field theory defining the model on $X$. Furthermore, we provide a novel interpretation of the sigma model’s one-loop beta function exclusively in terms of holomorphic data.

At the $(2,2)$ locus, the half-twisted variant of the topological B-model is represented by a mirror "Chiral de Rham complex" (CDR), as constructed by Malikov et al. in \cite{GMS1}. Employing mirror symmetry, we propose several conjectural relations linking the sheaf cohomology of the mirror CDR to that of the original CDR on pairs of Calabi–Yau mirror manifolds. Extending this analysis to the half-twisted model on a non-Kähler group manifold with torsion further permits inferences regarding the corresponding sheaves of CDR and their mirrors. These inferences align with the rigorously established results of Ben-Bassat \cite{ben} on mirror symmetry for generalized complex manifolds. Collectively, these findings underscore the fundamental role of the sheaf of CDR in advancing the theory of generalized mirror symmetry.

This paper synthesizes recent advancements in black hole accretion disk theory, underscoring the critical role of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) stresses in angular momentum transport. The frequent observation of accretion-driven outflows provides compelling evidence that large-scale MHD torques mediate vertical angular momentum transport. This mechanism significantly enhances the overall angular momentum removal rate, thereby facilitating matter accretion at appreciable rates. Furthermore, we argue that when vertical transport predominates, it alters the radial structure of the accretion disk at small radii, consequently modifying the disk’s emission spectrum. To elucidate this relationship, we present a simplified model demonstrating how energetic, magnetically driven outflows reshape the emergent disk emission spectrum relative to predictions from standard accretion disk theory. Comparative analysis of these theoretical spectra with observed quasar spectral energy distributions indicates that mass accretion rates inferred from the standard disk model may substantially underestimate their true values.

We investigate the phase structure of two-color, two-flavor QCD within the parameter space defined by the quark chemical potential \(\mu_q\) and the isospin chemical potential \(\mu_I\). Employing a mean-field framework, we self-consistently determine the chiral and diquark condensates, \(\sigma\) and \(\Delta\). In the chiral limit under weak coupling, we identify a specific interval for \(\mu_I\), \(0.71\Delta_0 < \mu_I < 0.75\Delta_0\), within which the single plane-wave Larkin-Ovchinnikov-Fulde-Ferrell (LOFF) phase is energetically favored over both the isotropic superfluid and normal quark matter phases. This LOFF window moderately broadens at elevated densities. Under stronger coupling and finite quark mass—conditions relevant to contemporary lattice two-color QCD simulations—the single plane-wave LOFF phase emerges only beyond a critical density threshold. Since the system is free from the fermion sign problem, these predictions regarding the LOFF region can be directly validated through lattice simulations. Further insight is afforded by constructing the energy landscape, which reveals local minima corresponding to the isotropic superfluid and LOFF phases, alongside a local maximum associated with the gapless phase. This analysis elucidates the transition pathway from the unstable gapless phase to the energetically favored LOFF phase.

Using the Rossi X-Ray Timing Explorer (RXTE), we conducted a monitoring campaign of the atoll-type neutron star low-mass X-ray binary 4U 1636-53 spanning over 1.5 years. The campaign comprised brief (~2 ks) observations at two-day intervals, facilitating systematic and continuous assessment of the source’s spectral and timing properties. During this period, we detected a pronounced long-term oscillation with a period of approximately 30–40 days, corroborating variability previously documented in RXTE All-Sky Monitor light curves. This oscillation corresponded to recurrent transitions between the hard (island) and soft (banana) spectral states. Kilohertz quasi-periodic oscillations (kHz QPOs) were identified in roughly one-third of the observations, predominantly during the soft (banana) state. Notably, the frequency distribution of the peak attributed to the lower kHz QPO diverges from that observed in an independent data set, indicating that the kHz QPOs in this system lack intrinsically preferred frequencies.

This study examines the distinguishability of multipartite quantum states under separable operations by establishing a necessary and sufficient condition for a finite set of orthogonal states to be distinguished via such operations. For the specific case of \((D-1)\) pure states, where \(D\) denotes the total dimension of the state space, we derive an explicit analytical formulation of this criterion. Building on this foundation, we explore several significant implications. In particular, we identify a broad class of \(2 \otimes 2\) separable operations that cannot be implemented through local operations and classical communication (LOCC), thereby extending prior results previously limited to a class of \(3 \otimes 3\) nonlocal separable operations [Bennett et al., Phys. Rev. A \textbf{59}, 1070 (1999)]. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any basis spanning the orthogonal complement of a multipartite pure state is indistinguishable by separable operations if and only if the state cannot be represented as a superposition of one or two orthogonal product states—that is, if its orthogonal Schmidt number is at least three. This finding generalizes earlier work on indistinguishable bipartite subspaces [Watrous, Phys. Rev. Lett. \textbf{95}, 080505 (2005)]. Finally, we provide explicit constructions of indistinguishable subspaces of dimension seven (or six) within composite quantum systems composed of two qutrits (or three qubits, respectively), thereby improving upon the previously known indistinguishable bipartite subspace of dimension eight.

We rigorously establish that, in the asymptotic long-time regime, a generic power-law waiting time distribution converges to the Mittag-Leffler distribution characteristic of time-fractional continuous-time random walks (CTRWs). This convergence results from the combined application of temporal rescaling and respeeding of the associated renewal process, followed by passage to a limit determined by a precise relationship between the rescaling and respeeding parameters. Extending this framework to spatially one-dimensional CTRWs with a generic power-law jump distribution, we interpret spatial rescaling as an additional form of respeeding. Under an appropriate parameter relation, this approach yields, in the limit, the space-time fractional diffusion equation. Finally, we characterize the time-fractional drift process as a properly scaled limit of the counting number associated with a Mittag-Leffler renewal process.

Utilizing Quantum Monte Carlo methods, we present the first comprehensive phonon spectra for a one-dimensional Heisenberg spin chain coupled to finite-frequency bond phonons, thereby elucidating the phonon dynamics within these systems.
